1qdnf7y.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 06, 2026Vulnerability / Windows Security A fix for CVE-2026-83844, a remote code execution flaw in Windows Paint, is now in the Microsoft Store. Paint gets this fix only through a Store update, not through Windows updates. The fixed build, 11.2609.401.0, was the newest Paint build in all ten countries The Hacker News checked today. The flaw is an out-of-bounds read that could let an attacker run code over a network. Microsoft rates it as Important, with a CVSS score of 8.1, and says that a successful attack requires a deep understanding of the target system. The flaw was not known to be exploited or publicly disclosed when the company published it on October 13. Brian Vitko of RFF, a device-management software maker, checked which Paint builds the Store offered in six countries earlier this week. He found that the newest in each was 11.2605.81.0, a build without the fix. His test virtual machine has since moved to the fixed build on its own, through Store auto-update. That is one machine, and how quickly other PCs will get the build is not yet clear. Which Build Counts as Fixed Microsoft's security advisory names 11.2609.401.0 as the fixed build. The CVE record for the flaw, which the company also publishes, still lists Paint as affected only below 11.2605.91.0. Its NVD entry shows the same range. So a scanner that reads the CVE record would treat any build from 11.2605.91.0 up as fixed. A copy at 11.2609.401.0 or later passes under both numbers. As recently as last week, the advisory gave 11.2605.91.0 as the fixed build, according to a forum question on Microsoft Q&A. The advisory's revision history still shows only its October 13 entry, with no note about the change. How to Check Every Copy of Paint Paint, like other Store apps, is installed separately for each user account on a PC. Windows can also keep a provisioned copy that it installs for each new user. A check of only the signed-in account can miss older copies. Vitko's test write-up gives two commands to run in a PowerShell window opened as administrator. The first lists every user's copy of Paint, and the second lists the provisioned copy. Get-AppxPackage -AllUsers -Name Microsoft.Paint | Select-Object Version, @{ n = 'Users'; e = { $_.PackageUserInformation.UserSecurityId.Username -join ', ' } } Get-AppxProvisionedPackage -Online | Where-Object DisplayName -eq 'Microsoft.Paint' | Select-Object Version For any copy below 11.2609.401.0: Update Paint through the Store, or let the Store auto-update install the fixed build. In Intune and other device-management tools, the Store app update scan does this across many PCs. Run both commands again and check that every copy shows 11.2609.401.0 or later. The advisory lists no workaround or mitigation. Before the fix reached the Store, Vitko suggested removing Paint where nobody needs it, for every user and from the provisioned copy. He did not test that step. Attack Conditions and Exploitation Status An attacker could exploit the flaw by sending "a specially crafted packet to an affected service over the network," the advisory says, but it does not name the service. The attack would require no sign-in and no user assistance. The flaw was not in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog run by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency when The Hacker News checked today. The catalog was last updated earlier this week.

vb4d4n.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 06, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Browser Security A browser extension that can run scripts on claude.ai could make Claude Desktop run code on a person's computer, researchers at Forever Security, an endpoint security company, showed in a test. The attack needs Dispatch, a Claude feature that lets people send tasks from their phone to Claude Desktop. The flaw that makes this possible can still be exploited, the researchers said earlier this week. Claude Desktop is an AI agent that can run commands on the computer where it is installed. The researchers found that Dispatch also accepted an ordinary signed-in session on claude.ai, the Claude website, even though the site showed no link to it. That let an extension running on the site send Claude Desktop instructions as if the user had sent them. The researchers say Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, told them on October 13 that Dispatch would be retired, with the end of October as the target. The Dispatch help page, last updated late last week, does not mention a retirement. It says Dispatch is closed to new users and that people who already use it on some Pro, Max, and Ultra plans "can keep using it for now." How the Attack Worked The attack needs two things, according to a technical write-up by Forever Security researcher Gal Weizman: an extension that can run scripts on claude.ai, and a person signed in to both claude.ai and Claude Desktop with Dispatch turned on. The extension could be malicious, a legitimate one that received a compromised update, or a legitimate one with a security flaw. Dispatch itself only works while the computer is awake and the desktop app is open. In the test, a script on the user's claude.ai page opened Dispatch and sent Claude four prompts as if it were the user. The prompts asked Claude to install an npm package. Claude first hesitated over the unfamiliar package, but a follow-up message, delivered in the user's voice, got it to go ahead. Claude asks before it acts, but those approval prompts appeared in the web page the extension controlled. The script clicked any "Allow" button every second, so no one had to be watching. Claude then ran a global npm install, and the package's install script opened the Calculator app. No browser exploit was needed. The same step could have stolen files or installed a backdoor, given Claude's permissions on the computer, the researchers say. The test was run with the browser and Claude Desktop on the same computer, and the researchers report no real attacks. Because Dispatch connects devices, the extension could also reach Claude Desktop on a different computer signed in to the same Claude account, they say. That case is described but not shown. The same reach could link a home computer to a work laptop when someone uses a single personal Claude account on both devices, with Dispatch turned on. The researchers have seen personal Claude accounts with cross-device Dispatch turned on, on work computers at their customers. The researchers reported the flaw to Anthropic on May 14. The company accepted it as valid on May 19 but closed the report as a duplicate of an issue it had already found internally, according to the researchers. "Anthropic is retiring Dispatch, but not the design behind it," the researchers wrote, adding that two other Claude features, Claude Code Remote Control and Claude Cowork sessions, let extensions carry out the same attack. Their write-up does not include a test of those features, and they plan a follow-up post. What Dispatch Users Can Do In Claude Desktop, Dispatch is part of Cowork and appears in the left-side panel. The Dispatch help page says users should know how to quickly disconnect or revoke access before turning the feature on, but it does not explain how. The researchers recommend these steps: Turn off cross-device Dispatch if you do not need it. If you do need it, review how devices are paired, approved, and removed. Treat browser extensions like other software on the computer: check their permissions, control what gets installed, and review updates that give them more access. Monitor what AI agents do on the computer, including unexpected package installations, setting changes, access to credentials, and external connections.

zw184o.text: An update on Athena, and some unsolicited predictions on what's coming next On Saturday, Dario Amodei published We Must Pace the Frontier. I agree with him. Go read it if you haven't. I've spent the summer looking at what these models find, and the gap he describes between what they can do and what the rest of us are ready for is the one I've been staring at since May. The hardest piece of his plan is the one that asks governments to coordinate. They're in a difficult spot: regulate too little and a US company accidentally builds the weapon, regulate too much and it gets built somewhere else, and open source isn't governable either way. Where governments can act is on consumption: not what the models can do, but what happens to what they find. Who gets a vulnerability first, how fast a fix reaches the people running the code, whether the operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline get a head start. That's what Gold Eagle is. It matters because of where the risk actually lands. The danger in Dario's essay isn't a model in a lab. It's a model pointed at the power grid, the water system, the hospital network, all of it running on decades of software with the same exploitable design. The frontier is where the capability comes from. Consumption is where it does damage, and that's the end you can still defend. So pacing has two ends. The frontier end is Dario's and the government's problem, and it's hard. The consumption end is ours: the disclosure processes, the patch pipelines, and the software itself, everything that has to absorb what the models produce. Pacing buys time on the frontier end. This post is a status report on how we're spending it, in three parts: We start disclosing Athena findings this month, beginning with 50. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing and are finding our own vulnerabilities, and I'll show you what that looks like. We built infrastructure to make both possible, and we're going to open it up. The short version: I'm more worried than I was in May, and more sure about what to do about it. The first 50 Athena has been taking in findings since June. The intake numbers are public: more than 40,000 findings, 42% of them critical or high, across more than 500 projects, with more than 2,000 patches produced. What hasn't been public is how much of that we've been sitting on. Generating fixes was never the bottleneck. Disclosing them responsibly, at a scale nobody has ever tried, is. On September 28, we start. We're beginning with about fifty, and none of them are the scary ones. That's deliberate. The frightening findings, the live pre-auth RCEs, go through Akrites on embargo, which I'll come back to. The first 50 are low-stakes on purpose: a small batch to get the flywheel turning and find out what breaks before the thousands behind them hit it. All 50 are silent fixes: vulnerabilities already fixed at head, sometimes years ago, where nobody ever filed a CVE. Your scanner has nothing to say about them, and the old versions are still running everywhere. This pattern showed up in Athena almost immediately. A big share of what the models find only affects old versions, because the models scan what's actually deployed, and what's deployed is old. Two systems fail at once with silent fixes, and neither is anyone's fault. Upstreams typically won't merge fixes to old versions, and they're right not to: the code was rewritten years ago, there's no branch to merge into, and "upgrade" is the correct answer. And the advisory layer has nothing to work with, because CVEs don't get filed for things already fixed at head. It's the one class of finding where acting doesn't step on anyone else's process, because there isn't one. For each one, where the project has no path for accepting fixes to old versions, we're doing three things. We publish the patch. Plain .patch files, in a public Chainguard repo that says exactly what it is on the tin, under the project's original license. This is deliberately not a maintainer-of-last-resort move. We have plans for that, and I'll get to them below, but they're for projects nobody maintains anymore. These are active projects that already fixed the bug at head. We're not forking anything, not claiming stewardship, not creating a new namespace, and not inviting anyone to build from it. It's a place to put patches for the people who can't upgrade yet, and nothing more. The durable fix is still upgrading, but this step reflects today's reality, where most of what's deployed isn't upgraded. We publish the advisory. A Chainguard OSV feed, with fully enumerated affected version ranges and the exact symbols affected. Not "some 2.x releases, probably." Athena partner scanners are integrating with it now, so these show up where your team already looks. We ship the fix. Patched versions land in Chainguard Libraries for every Chainguard customer the moment the advisory goes live. We're not planning to contact maintainers ahead of each of these. They already deal with more noise than anyone should, and we don't want to add to it, least of all for bugs they fixed years ago. If you maintain a project and you'd rather hear from us in advance going forward, or you have any other concerns about how this touches your project, let us know at cna@chainguard.dev and we'll happily work with you. We're becoming a CNA A silent fix used to be mostly harmless. Nobody had written the bug down, and finding it from a fix commit took real expertise and real time. That's over. A model can go from a public fix commit to a working exploit against every version that never got the fix in an afternoon. The finding exists whether we publish it or not. The only question is whether defenders get a copy, too. Once people know about a bug, the world needs a signal to upgrade, and the signal the world already has is the CVE. Scanners, KEV, and every compliance regime key on it. Silent fixes had none. So, in support of the Gold Eagle initiative, and in partnership with CISA, Chainguard is in progress to become a CVE Numbering Authority, scoped to open source vulnerabilities processed through Athena where upstream already fixed the flaw without an identifier, or where no maintainer is left to assign one, and no more specific CNA covers the project. The uncomfortable part: this will put new noise in your scanners. Old versions that scanned clean last week will light up. That's better than no noise and a breach. Silence in that channel was never safety, it was just nobody having looked yet. We also go to great lengths to keep each advisory as narrow as it can be. Every entry is enriched with the exact introduced and fixed ranges across every release branch, not a single version floor, and carries module, class, and function level detail on what's actually affected. That's what reachability scanners need to filter out the false positives for your codebase, so the noise you do see should be the noise that matters. The narrowness is the point. We assign only where there is no upstream to defer to. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, the project's own CNA assigns it, and we are the reporter, never the assigner. Every assignment clears the same gates: a reproduced finding, never raw model output; a defensible commit range; affected versions in real use; the maintainer notified with a response window; and withdrawal if the maintainer shows us we're wrong. Projects that become their own CNA leave our scope. This is a transitional role, not a territorial one. Where the rest goes The map for everything else is simple. If a vulnerability exists at the latest version and the maintainer is reachable, that's Plan A, and it runs through Akrites, the shared disclosure body the Linux Foundation launched in June, and that we helped found. If it exists at latest and the project is unmaintained, that's maintainer-of-last-resort territory, and we're working with other Akrites members to stand that up inside Akrites, where it belongs. And Gold Eagle, the federal clearinghouse that came out of June's executive order, is the layer that gets prioritized findings in front of the critical infrastructure operators who can't move on an attacker's timeline. We spent a good part of the summer waiting on both of those and helping build them. Akrites goes operational this month. I'll be straight about the tradeoff: one shared incident response team across dozens of organizations is slower at first than everyone acting alone. That's the cost of choosing "maintainers deal with one trusted counterpart" over "maintainers deal with thirty strangers," and we'd make it again. The disclosure and upstreaming numbers get published either way, pretty or not. A model found all of it in an afternoon The second reason I'm worried is less about process and more about what I've seen. We joined Anthropic's Project Glasswing. Lots of organizations have, at this point, roughly 200 across 15-plus countries, so our joining isn't news on its own. What matters is what it means for Athena: we now have Mythos, and we're running it against the software we build and ship. Here's the shape of one run, and I've picked it because it's the least reassuring result we have. One widely used open source project. One run, about six hours. The harness came back with more than a dozen validated vulnerabilities, most of them pre-authentication remote code execution, reachable with no credentials and no operator action. Every one was reproduced three times in a clean VM before it counted, under the rule I'll describe in a minute: the model doesn't get to claim a finding, the host has to reproduce it. This is not an abandoned package. It's one of the most heavily scanned, tested, and fuzzed projects in the ecosystem, code that has survived years of expert review and relentless fuzzing. A model found all of it in an afternoon. These go through Akrites like everyone else's findings, and I'm not going to say more about the specific project here than that. Here's what I'll say instead. Watching what these models find, and how long it takes a fix to reach anyone once they find it, is what worries me. It isn't the models themselves. It's the race between two clocks. On one, the industry is trying to absorb a short-term rush of findings through disclosure processes that were already behind. On the other, attacker capability is advancing toward the point where compromising critical infrastructure at scale becomes cheap. Right now, the second clock is running faster than the first, and I don't see anything that closes that gap on its own. Sandboxes and sandboxing Which is the other reason the sandbox matters. Producing a finding like the one above means building and detonating a working exploit against real code, over and over, driven by an agent nobody is watching in real time. That is dangerous to run, and this summer has been a run of examples of people running it unsafely. The incident Dario built his essay around, OpenAI's agents breaking out of a cyber evaluation and ending up inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure, started with a zero-day in the package cache the agents had been given. Package infrastructure is what we build, so that one landed close to home. Pillar Security spent a week in July publishing sandbox escapes across Cursor, Codex, Gemini CLI, and Antigravity, and the finding that tied them together was that the agent almost never broke the sandbox head-on. It wrote a file it was allowed to write, and something trusted outside the box ran it later. None of these was a problem of insufficient sandboxes. They were a problem of insufficient sandboxing: the boundary existed, and everything interesting happened in the gaps around it. Denylists don't contain any better than containers do. Everything Athena does, from developing an exploit to proving a patch closes the hole, runs inside a microVM, the same primitive our package builds, image builds, and CI have run on for years. Matt wrote up the architecture in July. The short version: every job gets a hardware-virtualized guest with its own kernel and a root filesystem built from scratch, egress is enforced at the hypervisor and allowlisted to package registries and nothing else, the first forbidden connection destroys the VM, and no credentials ever enter the guest. And because a shared primitive multiplies the blast radius of any weakness, we point AI agents at the sandbox itself with instructions to break it. Every finding lands as a failing test first, then the fix. The harness starts with a person The harness that runs inside those sandboxes is the part I find most interesting, and it starts with a person. Ian Beer spent about six months writing a zero-click iOS exploit chain, and if you read the write-up as a search, you can see the shape of it: poke at a target, go deep, hit a dead end, back up, eventually connect enough dots to reach a working exploit. No human holds six months of that in working memory. He kept it in notes and pulled back the slice he needed each session. His notebook was the environment. That's what we built, sharded across many agents in parallel: a tree search where every agent starts fresh with a scoped surface and a distilled trail of what's already known, and continuity lives in durable findings rather than anyone's context window. The rule I care most about is that the host casts the vote, never the model. A finding only counts if the host can replay it against a clean instance: the check fails before, the replay runs, the check passes after. Nothing enters the record until reality agrees, and that one rule is most of why the false positive rate is as low as it is. A few things we learned building this, if you're working on something similar: Fresh context, bounded job. Every agent starts clean with a scoped surface. Continuity lives in findings written for a stranger, not a transcript. Every write gated on evidence. Without a precondition, a postcondition, and a host-runnable replay, it doesn't enter the record. Research steers, it doesn't prove. It decides where an agent looks next and never counts as a finding. Record dead ends as findings, too. A false positive collides with reality and starves on its own. A false negative is silent, permanent, and the failure that actually costs you the deep bugs. Taste beats fleet size. In a search like this, the model's per-step judgment about where to look is the base of an exponent, and parallelism only shows up inside a logarithm. You cannot buy your way out of worse taste with more agents. That's the concrete, non-marketing reason we wanted Mythos, and why Glasswing matters more than how many agents you can run. Put the pieces together, and the loop closes. Find, contain, fix, ship. All of it on one primitive. What we built to do this, and what we're opening up None of this was possible on off-the-shelf infrastructure. Over the last year, we rebuilt our factory on three new primitives, and every one of them started as something we needed for ourselves before it was anything we could sell. The sandbox is the microVM you just read about: the isolation boundary that lets us run untrusted code and hostile agents without the blast radius reaching anything that matters. The harness is the search that runs inside it, the thing that found those pre-auth RCEs. And the third is CI as a function: our own fleet stopped sending code out to a CI system a year ago. The checks run in the loop, and changes arrive already proven, at more than ten times the CVE volume we were handling before. We built all three because we had to; we've been running our entire operation on them, and over the coming quarters, we're going to start opening them up directly. If you are running untrusted AI workloads, or trying to find real vulnerabilities in your own code, or drowning in CI that tells you less than you'd like, these are the tools we reached for. Soon you'll be able to reach for them too. So what is the endgame here? Here's the unsolicited prediction. Everyone is worried about Mythos zero-days right now, and almost nobody was keeping up with ordinary CVEs before any of this started. The median enterprise is months behind on patches that have had fixes, advisories, and scanner coverage for years. That's the system we're about to pour thousands of new findings into. Faster disclosure and faster patching only help the people who can move on them, and most of the world can't move at the speed a model sets. If you take one thing from this post, take this: the flood is coming, and the pipes were already full. Which is why none of the above is the finish line. Everything in this post makes us faster, and all of it accepts a losing premise: that the goal is to keep pace with a discovery rate set by frontier models. The vulnerability classes those models exploit aren't defects in today's software. They're its design. Memory corruption, deserialization, injection, confused deputies: consequences of how the stacks under every enterprise application were built. You cannot patch your way out of an architecture. So the endgame is new foundations: a stack built secure by construction, where the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written in the first place, filling the role Spring Boot fills today, across every enterprise language, underneath the frameworks and the registries they pull from. For forty years, migration costs protected every incumbent platform. Nobody rewrote the COBOL because nobody could afford to. Agents just collapsed that cost. We're working on this, and I'll say more when there's more to say. Why us: we see the world's pre-disclosure findings before almost anyone, so we know which bug classes matter, and we have the one tool that can prove a foundation removed them. Point Mythos at it before you ship, and you know. Dario is right that pacing buys time, and everything above is how we're spending it. But a paced frontier only matters if the software underneath survives the frontier we already have. If the dominant vulnerability classes can't be written, the critical infrastructure built on them can't be broken by them, and a frontier model in the wrong hands has far less to reach. Pacing limits the risk by slowing the capability. Foundations limit it by taking away the target, and that's the only version of this I can see that ends the treadmill instead of running faster on it. The Programmer's Credo says we do these things not because they are easy, but because we thought they would be easy when we started. This is the first one where I didn't even think that. We're doing it anyway. If you maintain a project any of this touches, or if you're finding vulnerabilities, join at chainguard.dev/athena. And if any of this sounds like something you want to build, we're hiring.

1421zur.text: Cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask said a recent security incident has not affected MetaMask wallets or its wallet infrastructure. The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet (developed by blockchain software company Consensys) lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and compatible blockchains. MetaMask revealed on September 30 that it was investigating an "ongoing infrastructure security incident" and exited affected validators (Ethereum network nodes responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining Ethereum blockchain security) within non-custodial staking operations. While the company shared almost no details at the time and redirected BleepingComputer to the public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected, in a Thursday update it said that a threat actor gained access to systems used to store recipient addresses and diverted some execution-layer staking rewards. "The issue was identified and addressed on the same day, and approximately 0.385 ETH in rewards was diverted. These rewards are separate from customers' staked ETH," MetaMask said. "We have found no evidence that customers' staked principal or withdrawal keys were compromised, and the affected systems have been secured." It also added that the attack did not compromise MetaMask users' Secret Recovery Phrases or private keys and that it was working with affected customers to refund the lost rewards. "Some customers have experienced temporary withdrawal delays as a result of the precautionary validator exits. The process may also have resulted in missed staking rewards while validators were exiting or awaiting reactivation. We are working directly with affected customers and partners to address any outstanding impact," MetaMask noted. "MetaMask wallet users do not need to take any action as a result of this incident. Customers whose staking arrangements were affected should follow any guidance provided directly by MetaMask or their staking provider." Last month, Ledger also asked Asian resellers and distributors to halt wallet sales and remove products from shelves while it was investigating multiple hardware implant incidents. More recently, crypto exchange Binance confirmed that North Korean hackers stole $6.34 billion after compromising its wallet infrastructure by tricking an employee into installing malware in a fake job interview. 1b2skzs.text: Blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis has revealed that its ongoing investigation into the agentic cyber attack targeting its systems also exposed names, usernames, password hashes and live tokens for all users. "While we investigated, we removed access to Reactor and Data Solutions," the company said. "At this time we continue to have no evidence that any investigations data has been accessed or Chainalysis attribution data has been manipulated." Chainalysis said it has implemented additional proactive monitoring systems to detect unusual activity, adding it took the Know Your Transaction (KYT) user interface and API offline, alongside other address screening products and the login page. Previously, Chainalysis said it was probing what it described as an "ongoing multi-front cyber attack," leading to the discovery of an "on-path attack" that exposed a subset of customer passwords. The company said the attack vector has since been addressed. Out of an abundance of caution, Chainalysis has also taken the step of locking the impacted accounts. "For customers who just received an email from us instructing you to reset your Chainalysis password, resetting this password won't be possible right now," it noted. "We still encourage you, where necessary, to reset your password on other systems where you may be reusing credentials." The development comes less than a week after Chainalysis said it was the target of a cybersecurity incident in which an external actor leveraged offensive agentic techniques to obtain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools. The company said it intends to begin restoring access to KYT and Address Screening, urging customers to contact its support email (support@chainalysis.com) or their Chainalysis account team with trusted IP addresses, which will be added to an allowlist. From there, users can reset their passwords and rotate API keys to register transactions. "We are working around the clock to harden our systems and bring Reactor and Data Solutions back online," Chainalysis said. "We will require additional protections to access accounts, including that every user will have to reset passwords and rotate API keys as appropriate. We will communicate these changes as necessary." It's unclear who is behind the attack, but Chainalysis notes it was similar to "many other tech platforms in recent weeks." Rise in AI-Linked Attacks Indeed, a number of companies, including Chainstack, OpenCode, Warp, and WorkOS, have disclosed that they have been targeted by artificial intelligence (AI)-driven attacks, some of which involve an autonomous penetration testing tool called ARTEX. According to Microsoft, threat actors are using an agentic AI offensive framework to search public GitHub repositories for exposed secrets, such as credentials, application credentials, and AI inference-related API keys across multiple applications and cloud services, to conduct follow-on attacks. "Agentic tooling like ARTEX allows threat actors to not only scan for secrets across multiple repositories at a quicker pace but also use the agents to analyze the output and conduct follow-on attacks, cutting down on the need for the threat actor to have hands-on-keyboard interactions throughout the attack chain," the tech giant said. In at least one case, an AI agent is said to have progressed from scanning GitHub for secrets to exfiltrating data from Azure Key Vault in just five minutes. The activity is assessed to be ongoing from August 2026. Some aspects of the campaign correspond to post-exploitation activity involving the misuse of valid application credentials to access Microsoft Entra ID tenants of certain organizations and connected Azure and Microsoft 365 resources. The sign-in events originated from two IP addresses, 199.19.77[.]84 and 199.19.77[.]18. "The agent successfully conducted service principal sign-ins on dozens of associated applications across multiple tenants," Microsoft said. "The threat actor targeted operations that return credentials, including storage account keys, App Service settings, connection strings and publishing credentials, AI and machine learning (ML) connections and datastores, and Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) user credentials. The compromised applications subsequently accessed SharePoint and OneDrive in the targeted organization tenants, including file downloads and mailbox-item access." In addition, the threat actor has been observed attempting to steal Azure resources, including compromised Azure AI services, likely as part of efforts to facilitate broader attack activity. Another notable aspect of the campaign is that the agentic AI tools have been found obtaining a token for a single-tenant OAuth application in the same target organization, then use the compromised OAuth application to enumerate other cloud resources within the organization. In a handful of cases, Microsoft said it observed the agents exfiltrating secrets from the organization's Azure Key Vault. "During this activity, the AI agents repeatedly demonstrated a focus on credentials that provide access to AI services, such as API keys for major AI service providers and OAuth applications with access to Foundry Tools (previously known as Azure Cognitive Services)," Microsoft said. The development also coincides with a surge in attacks targeting AI developer platforms over the past month, allowing threat actors to resell access, abuse them as free compute (i.e., LLMjacking), and use them as attribution cover for further attacks. In a report published this week, Google disclosed that cybercriminals have established a business model out of stealing cloud access to commercial large language models (LLMs) and reselling it to paying customers. The monetization infrastructure centers on LLM Mixers, who act as an illicit intermediary to advertise access to compromised enterprise LLM accounts on underground markets without their customers needing to set up their own legitimate API credentials or cloud infrastructure. In other words, LLM mixers turn stolen enterprise model access into a criminal routing gateway for paying subscribers, while the legitimate owner's systems continue to accept requests. These services help proxy requests across stolen accounts, distribute consumption, and obscure the original source of access. The emerging LLMjacking ecosystem "create[s] a market that makes the theft easily monetizable, likely driving more actors to undertake operations to steal credentials," Wiz said. The Google-owned subsidiary also said it identified at least two resale operations leveraging stolen AWS Bedrock keys obtained from two different organizations – llm-routing[.]com (momo) and xingjiabiapi[.]org – both of which offer a wide selection of frontier models for discount prices. That said, there is no evidence that the operators of these websites were responsible for the initial platform compromises. Interestingly, the IP address linked to llm-routing[.]com, 23.106.46[.]239, hosted an Artex landing page in mid-October 2026 and has been flagged by Zeabur as an indicator of compromise. Last month, Zeabur disclosed a security breach in which an unknown threat actor exploited credentials stored in plaintext to compromise its infrastructure, exfiltrating over 3.2 million environment variable records and data associated with 321,810 accounts. The following IP addresses have been used to test stolen keys and are suspected to be linked to LLM token abuse and resale - 23.106.46.239 38.246.114.118 104.243.32.50 31.57.201.201 "Threat actors are not only using AI as a tool to conduct attacks, they are also compromising victim environments solely to abuse their finances for mass Large Language Model (LLM) execution, incurring hundreds of thousands of dollars in AI API charges," Wiz said.

1kfqvym.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 06, 2026Malware / Web Security A backdoor has been found hiding in the web server that runs Control Web Panel (CWP), a free panel for managing Linux hosting servers, researchers at QiAnXin's XLab said this week. The backdoored web server executes commands that attackers send via web requests, and those requests never appear in its access logs. Installing it takes root access, so the attackers must already control the server. The researchers, who named the backdoor cwpdoor, captured its installer, a shell script posing as a version update, on June 29. The installer handles only two versions of that web server, cwpsrv 1.15.10 and 1.24.0. The researchers do not yet know how attackers get the root access the installer needs. On September 30, an archive holding a copy of the backdoor was uploaded to VirusTotal from Brazil. The researchers say this indicates that "real victims already exist in the wild." They give no count of infected servers. The backdoor is cwpsrv itself, rebuilt with extra code, the researchers found in their technical analysis. It behaves like the normal program until a request arrives with a valid timestamp and signature in custom headers whose names begin with X-Ngx-Integrity. It then runs the command carried in the request. When the installer replaces the cwpsrv file, it puts the file's dates back to their original values, so checks with ls and stat show it as unchanged. When the researchers checked, the backdoor file had zero detections out of 63 on VirusTotal. Checking a Server for the Backdoor XLab gives three checks: Socket: run ss -axp | grep integrity. A result naming ngx_http_integrity_helper, the Unix socket the backdoor uses, is a sign of infection. Process: run ps aux | grep cwpsrv and look for unexpected helper processes started by cwpsrv. File: run strings /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin/cwpsrv | grep X-Ngx-Integrity and look for the backdoor's header names. In the researchers' example, the socket check found the backdoor on a server where the list of open ports looked normal. The researchers published these indicators: MD5: e505d4ffa21cf494a5dc2d7c8f4f1236 (installer script, cwpsrv_update.sh) MD5: 965aea67fb40de1bab5169ada993349f (backdoored cwpsrv 1.15.10) MD5: d3f4e95113d49ab3991b45e457bda75b (backdoored cwpsrv 1.24.0) IP: 136.0.141[.]71 (download server) URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_update.sh URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.15.10 URL: https://136.0.141[.]71/static/cwpsrv_1.24.0 Cleaning Up an Infected Server If a server is infected, the researchers recommend three steps: Restore the original cwpsrv from the backup the installer creates in /usr/local/cwpsrv/bin, with a name starting cwpsrv.prev- and ending in a date and time. The researchers' description of the installer says it deletes "the temporary files and backup" after a successful swap, so this copy may be missing. Upgrade to the latest version, then confirm that ss -axp | grep integrity returns nothing. Change all control panel credentials, because the backdoor can run any command. Treat the whole server as compromised and check it for other threats. The archive uploaded from Brazil also held the Ebury malware, an OpenSSH backdoor and credential stealer active since at least 2009. The researchers do not know whether the two are related, and say different attackers may have planted them on the same server.

i2j48a.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 06, 2026Vulnerability / Email Security Two flaws in Barracuda's Email Security Gateway, an email-filtering appliance, can be chained to run commands on it as root, its highest level of access, with no login required. The company released patches on Monday, and the security firm watchTowr detailed the attack chain on Thursday. One flaw, CVE-2026-116606, is an authorization bypass. An unauthenticated attacker can use it to restore a crafted configuration backup and change the appliance's global settings. The other, CVE-2026-111560, is a command injection. It runs commands as root but normally needs an administrator account, and on the Email Security Gateway the bypass gives an attacker that access. Chained, the two let an attacker reach root with no login. Affected Products and Fixes The authorization bypass affects only the Email Security Gateway. The command injection reaches five other products, but on those it still needs an administrator account. Mandiant, which assigned the two CVE records, rates the bypass 9.3 out of 10 and the command injection 8.6. Barracuda has released a patch for each affected product and lists the fixed firmware in its security advisory. The Email Security Gateway is fixed in version 9.4.0.030 and later. What to Do The advisory sets out three steps: Apply the patch for each affected product, or upgrade to the fixed firmware listed above. If you cannot patch at once, limit the appliance's administration interface to trusted internal networks. If you have turned automatic patching off, switch it back on. How the Chain Works In its technical analysis, watchTowr traced the chain through the appliance's code. A failed password change returns the attacker a low-privilege role instead of stopping the request, which leaves a backup-restore function open to someone who has not logged in. That function accepts an uploaded backup, and the restored data includes a timezone value that the appliance later runs as a shell command with root privileges. Barracuda guards backups with a checksum, but the secret used to compute it is built into the code, allowing an attacker to forge a valid checksum. The firm showed the attack by writing a file to the appliance as root. As of this week, neither flaw appears in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV catalog), and no public report ties either to an attack. watchTowr also released a detection tool that checks whether an appliance is vulnerable, but has not published an exploit. The Email Security Gateway was hit in the 2023 attacks by a group tracked as UNC4841, which exploited a different flaw, CVE-2023-2868, as a zero-day. That case is unrelated to the two flaws patched this week, and nothing ties the new pair to any attacker.

ot0ee5.text: The FBI and CISA warn that hackers are actively targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide, potentially causing food spoilage, equipment damage, and fire hazards. The warning was issued jointly with the U.S. Departments of Health and Human Services (HHS), Agriculture (USDA), and Transportation (DOT), urging critical infrastructure operators to secure vulnerable refrigeration controllers used in healthcare, food production, chemical facilities, and transportation. "Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target," said Chris Butera, CISA's Acting Executive Assistant Director for Cybersecurity. According to a joint advisory published Thursday, attackers are exploiting weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration management systems. These devices allow operators to monitor temperatures remotely, manage defrost cycles, and control cooling equipment. "Globally, malicious cyber actors are targeting vulnerabilities and weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible electronic temperature controllers and commercial refrigeration controllers in retail grocery and cold storage facilities," CISA warned. The agencies say attackers may exploit authentication bypass vulnerabilities, arbitrary code injection flaws, or weak configurations to modify temperature settings and force refrigeration equipment into continuous heating or defrost cycles. Successful attacks can cause inventory losses, reduce equipment lifespan, create fire hazards, and create unsafe storage conditions. Attackers may also reduce visibility into current temperatures, preventing operators from detecting problems. The warning follows a series of attacks against European refrigeration systems that have disrupted supermarkets and blood storage facilities. In October, hackers compromised refrigeration controllers at an estimated 250 to 350 French supermarkets, remotely activating defrost functions and raising temperatures in refrigerators and freezers. A second wave of attacks reported in November affected more than 115 stores across six European countries, with some refrigeration systems shutting down entirely and others raising temperatures to as high as 50°C (122°F). On November 3, the French Blood Establishment (EFS) confirmed that a cybersecurity incident affecting a refrigeration equipment provider had altered temperature and defrost settings at three facilities used to store blood products. In response to the ongoing threat, the U.S. agencies are urging organizations to remove refrigeration controllers from the public internet, secure necessary remote access, change default passwords, and apply available security updates. They also recommend isolating operational technology systems from business networks and enforcing safe temperature limits to prevent controllers from operating outside acceptable ranges. csv6pp.text: The European Commission accused TikTok on Friday of failing to prevent its recommendation algorithm from drawing users into “rabbit holes” of content about sadness, self-harm and body image. The preliminary findings that TikTok violated the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA) come amid focus on both sides of the Atlantic on whether and how social media platforms are endangering young users. European officials said their findings were the first time EU regulators have directly challenged the engagement-based recommendation system of a major social media platform, and, to their knowledge, was the first enforcement action of its kind worldwide. The investigation was directly “addressing a business model” built primarily on user engagement, a Commission official told journalists. TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed “shows users a continuous stream of personalised videos, even when those are related to mental health struggles and body image,” stated the European Commission. “The more a user interacts with a certain type of content, the more TikTok’s ‘For You’ feed algorithm recommends similar content. This design can be harmful when such endless and repeated exposure involves, for example, content about sadness, isolation or body image.” Brussels said TikTok had identified some of the issues it was flagging in its own risk assessments, but that its investigators found the company had failed to properly analyze those risks and set appropriate safeguards. The findings are not final and TikTok has a chance to review the Commission’s evidence and challenge its findings. If the DSA violations are confirmed the company could face a fine of up to 6% of its annual global revenue. The company does not publish its global revenue, nor does its parent company ByteDance. Rabbit holes European officials stressed the case was not about removing content, and said investigators deliberately focused on videos that were neither illegal nor against TikTok’s own rules, which one official described as the “least harmful” category of content. Citing trends including “what I eat in a day” and “SkinnyTok,” officials said the legal content could appear harmless in isolation but became damaging through repetition, particularly for young and vulnerable users. It follows U.S. senators in August demanding answers from TikTok over the death of Chase Nasca, a 16-year-old who took his own life in February 2022 after viewing a stream of content related to sadness and suicide. An internal TikTok review, reported last year by Bloomberg, revealed Nasca was part of a control group comprising about 10% of the platform’s user base in which it withheld design changes intended to prevent repeated exposure to harmful subjects. “If you get a chain of hundreds or even thousands of videos of the same kind of content, this drives people in what we call a rabbit hole, and this has a negative impact on people's mental well-being,” a European Commission official said on Friday. TikTok’s own tools to break the loops do not work, according to the Commission, which said the platform’s “dispersion” techniques to diversify the feed are ineffective, refreshing the feed only helps briefly, and tapping “not interested” stops working after a while. In particular, the Commission said it wants TikTok to base its algorithmic recommendations on what users explicitly say they want rather than on implicit signals such as how long they view videos for. They said they spent two and a half years developing “amongst the world’s most advanced investigatory infrastructures,” but that specific testing methods were necessarily secret to prevent platforms from gaming the tools. They said they obtained the company’s internal documents and data, and analyzed around 20,000 videos with help from psychologists, psychiatrists and experts in system design. The testing “didn't really need access to the exact algorithm. We had enough information without it,” one official said. A spokesperson for TikTok, which has the right to check and challenge the Commission’s evidence, said: “The Commission has made a series of statements that are fundamentally inaccurate and distort our platform’s architecture and our commitment to user safety. “We have a strong record of protecting our community while giving users direct and intuitive control over their content experience,” they added. Friday’s findings are the third the Commission has issued against TikTok this year, following one in February challenging addictive design features and another in July regarding protections on minors’ accounts. Officials distinguished this case as being focused on the platform’s recommendation system rather than issues related to notifications or endless scrolling. They said it went further than TikTok’s recent settlement in Alabama, which “does not go as deep” into the recommendation system. They acknowledged other platforms similarly push users into rabbit holes and said the Commission was “looking more widely beyond TikTok,” although they declined to comment beyond TikTok. The Commission described the case as a “scene setter” for its proposed KIDS Act, introduced in September, which would prohibit platforms from relying solely on engagement signals to recommend content to children — a provision officials said was directly inspired by its TikTok investigation. ka9p4n.text: Hackers are using fake OpenAI, SpaceX, and Anthropic event invitations to lure employees into phishing attacks, using two different phishing-as-a-service platforms to steal Microsoft and Google account credentials and authentication sessions. According to a new report from Push Security, the attackers use convincing event registration pages offering free access to premium AI services and other rewards to trick victims into signing in with their corporate accounts. What makes the attacks interesting is that the same phishing pages integrate two separate phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) platforms, Kali365 and VoidProxy, to target Microsoft and Google accounts using different authentication attacks. Kali365 conducts Microsoft device code phishing attacks, while VoidProxy acts as an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) reverse proxy to intercept Google sign-ins and steal authentication session cookies. The Microsoft attack also uses VoidProxy as a second stage, allowing attackers to capture credentials and session cookies after obtaining authentication tokens through Kali365. Push Security says it detected and blocked visits to the malicious event registration pages in late October 2026. The campaign comes after a similar campaign documented by ANY.RUN in July, when attackers abused legitimate Zoom event pages to promote fake Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic events that led to device code and AiTM phishing attacks. Cofense also recently reported on phishing emails impersonating Anthropic event invitations that were distributed through GoTo Webinar's email infrastructure and redirected recipients through multiple websites to fake registration pages. Fake AI events lead to account phishing While it is unclear how the attackers initially distribute the phishing links, Push Security found that they redirect victims to a malicious event registration page using links from trusted services, including Google and Zapier URL shorteners. Invitations from earlier versions of the campaign were also distributed through GoTo Webinar's email systems or legitimate Zoom event pages. Push Security says the attackers use two custom phishing kits, tracked as ZoomMock and MSDRoot, to create fake event pages that then direct victims to the Kali365 and VoidProxy phishing services. The researchers believe the same threat actors operate both kits, as they use shared infrastructure and the same targeting. The campaign impersonates events hosted by OpenAI, SpaceX, and Anthropic, with registration pages designed to resemble legitimate event websites. One phishing page advertises an OpenAI event titled "ChatGPT for Social & Digital Marketing Teams" that promises three months of ChatGPT Pro to participants. OpenAI phishing page Source: BleepingComputer Another promotes a private SpaceX event on November 12, offering registrants either three months of Grok Heavy or a "SpaceX share." The researchers also found a phishing page impersonating an Anthropic event at AWS re:Invent 2026 that was already taken down. The fake registration pages tell visitors they must sign in with their work accounts to register and claim the advertised rewards. Before displaying the fake registration pages, the websites show a Cloudflare CAPTCHA to "Confirm you're not a robot." This prevents automated security platforms from scanning the phishing site. Once visitors reach the event registration page, they see two options: "Continue with Microsoft" and "Continue with Google." When victims select the Microsoft option, the phishing page contacts the Kali365 platform to generate a Microsoft device authentication code. Microsoft device code authentication form on phishing site Source: BleepingComputer A device code phishing attack occurs when an attacker abuses the legitimate OAuth 2.0 device authorization grant flow to obtain authentication tokens for the victim's Microsoft Entra account. This can then be used to access the user's resources and connected SSO applications, such as Microsoft 365, Salesforce, Google Workspace, Dropbox, Adobe, SAP, Slack, Zendesk, Atlassian, and many others. Device code phishing attacks have been used in the past for data theft and cyberespionage attacks. The visitor is instructed to copy the code and enter it on Microsoft's legitimate device login website, where they authenticate and approve the request. This allows the Kali365 phishing platform to steal Microsoft authentication tokens without requiring the victim to disclose their password directly. After the device code authentication succeeds, the page redirects the victim to a VoidProxy Microsoft login page, where attackers can also capture the victim's password and session cookie. When victims select the Google authentication option, the phishing page instead opens a pop-up containing a Google login page from the VoidProxy PhaaS. The platform operates as an adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) platform that sits between the victim's browser and Google's login page, proxies the login forms, and steals credentials, MFA responses, and session cookies. Both the Kali365 and VoidProxy platforms let attackers bypass multifactor authentication by capturing an already authenticated session or, in the case of device code authentication, bypassing MFA entirely. To protect against these attacks, employees should avoid entering Microsoft device authentication codes provided by unfamiliar websites and be cautious of event invitations that require signing in with corporate accounts to claim rewards. Organizations can also restrict device code authentication where it is not needed and use phishing-resistant MFA, such as FIDO2 security keys, to help prevent session hijacking. v2mt5j.text: Truffle Security has launched the Secrets Revocation Program, a free initiative that helps API key issuers revoke 1.4 million publicly exposed secrets that remain valid. Since 2022, the company has discovered secrets embedded in public repositories, packages, container images, datasets, and applications. Earlier this year, Truffle Security reported that it had found 543,000 valid credentials leaked in public GitHub repositories. In a separate investigation, the company identified more than 431,000 AWS secrets across code repositories, Git histories, datasets, Docker images, registries, and CI logs. These secrets are typically exposed by mistake during the development process, by committing credentials to a public repository, including them in published Docker images or packages, or leaving them in configuration files uploaded with an app or dataset. Truffle Security says that the problem is that the owners of these secrets are not responsive to researchers’ notifications about leaked data. “Telling developers their keys leaked doesn’t get them turned off: 81% of the keys we reported last year still worked six months later,” the company explained. As a result, exposed secrets pose unnecessary security risks that can extend beyond the affected companies to their customers and downstream application users. Accumulation of valid exposed keys over time Source: Truffle Security The researchers note that the rise of AI coding tools has only worsened the situation, increasing secrets exposure even more. “Since January 2025 we’ve found 2,655 working keys in AI coding tools’ config files like that one,” the researchers said, noting that this was a non-existent problem the year before. AI is also increasing the impact of exposure on the offensive side, as shown by OpenAI’s July incident, where AI agents used exposed Hugging Face tokens to steal data from the platform. Revoking exposed keys Truffle’s new program, which uses the TruffleHog tool to check for the validity of leaked keys, aims to coordinate the revocation of exposed secrets with the entities that issued them. Truffle says it can either use a revocation endpoint provided by those entities, or supply them with the verified keys through a webhook and revoke them within 14 days. This way, even when owners are unresponsive, the keys can be invalidated. Key removal procedure Source: Truffle Security Sixteen issuers have already joined the program, including Hugging Face, Notion, Vercel, Resend, RubyGems, and Twilio. Truffle says the unilateral revocation approach can be very effective, as demonstrated by Google when it began disabling exposed Google Cloud service-account keys by default on June 16, 2024. When Google relied only on notifying key owners, Truffle Security found that many customers failed to respond, leaving 72% of the exposed secrets active. By automatically disabling leaked keys, the figure was reduced to 11%. Although eliminating all valid exposed keys is impossible because customers can opt out of automatic revocation, the measure proved to be effective. mn1j3v.text: OpenAI disclosed that its GPT-6 Astra frontier model sometimes hindered safety research by complicating simple tasks, abandoning viable approaches, and silently refusing researchers’ requests. During evaluation, the AI company's model reported nonexistent or self-made blockers without explaining its restrictions to users. OpenAI said it first received a report of what it calls "covert underperformance" in Astra on August 20. The company then conducted targeted evaluations to investigate the behavior and determine its causes, noting that it had not observed the same issue in GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI says it received the first report of what it calls “covert underperformance” in Astra on August 20. The company then ran specifically designed evaluation experiments to determine the extent and cause of this behavior, noting that the issues were not observed in GPT-5.6 Sol. “Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing,” reads OpenAI’s report. “This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison.” A rubric item is one specific requirement used to score the model’s work, essentially an item on a grading checklist. Source: OpenAI The main issue is that instead of explicitly declaring its inability to help with a research task and explaining its limitations to users, the model silently quits when it considers the work unsafe. The concern is that researchers may trust results the model silently changed or left incomplete, misleading safety testing and wasting valuable research time. OpenAI provided eight specific examples of this behavior, drawn from internal evaluations. These include avoiding a retry fix that would improve a training pipeline, restricting exploit-development assistance, excluding a violent source from a safety evaluation, and limiting jailbreak-data exports. OpenAI hypothesized that training intended to produce safer behavior may have encouraged undisclosed obstruction of safety work. However, it has not established this as the definitive cause for the observed model’s behavior. The company also located a grader, a tool that evaluates AI model performance during reinforcement learning, that favored covert withholding over explicit refusal. However, it did not conclusively establish this as the cause.
