17vjjnd.text: Attackers can log in to accounts that have no password, such as SSH key-only accounts, on some Alpine Linux servers running the standard openssh-server package. They need network access to the server, an account name, and a password between 257 and 1,024 bytes long. OpenSSH, which rates the flaw critical, released version 10.6p2 today to block it. Alpine has published fixed packages for every release back to 3.16. The attack works when the OpenSSH server (sshd) checks passwords without the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface, password logins are enabled, and at least one other account on the machine has a password. Alpine's openssh-server package is built without PAM, and password logins are on by default. The flaw comes from how sshd works with musl, the C library that Alpine is built on. Non-Linux systems, Linux systems built on glibc, and systems that check passwords through PAM are not affected, said Damien Miller of the OpenSSH project. He told anyone running an affected system to "set PasswordAuthentication=no or disable SSH for these systems IMMEDIATELY." No attacks using the flaw have been reported. Who Is Exposed Alpine's security advisory lists four conditions. A server is exposed when all four are true: It runs the openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or runs openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. PasswordAuthentication is yes, which is the OpenSSH default. An account has * as its password field, which means no password is set. At least one other local account has a password hash starting with $5$ or $6$. The attacker also needs the name of an account with no password. One account with a password is enough to expose every account without one. The attack succeeds on every try with a single connection, according to the advisory. On Alpine, accounts with no password set include: key-only users created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*' users who come from a directory service through musl-nscd, since they have no shadow entry root, which has shipped as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16 the alpine user in the official cloud images built with tiny-cloud Root is protected by the default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password setting and can be reached directly only if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That protection does not help if an exposed account can become root, for example through doas. The tiny-cloud images from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 give the alpine user passwordless doas. They are safe at first boot but become open to attack once any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example after an admin sets a console password. An attacker can then log in as alpine and use doas to become root. Containers that do not run sshd, systems with PasswordAuthentication no, and cloud images set up through cloud-init, which writes that setting, are not affected. Accounts locked with ! in /etc/shadow are not affected either, and neither are machines where no account has a $-style password hash. The flaw is not limited to Alpine. Özgün Kültekin of Wakefield, who reported it, names OpenWrt, Buildroot and Yocto in his technical write-up as other musl-based systems to check. OpenWrt handles SSH with Dropbear by default, as its Dropbear documentation shows, and Kültekin says Dropbear is not affected. On OpenWrt, the flaw can matter only where an admin has installed the OpenSSH server. How to Fix It On Alpine, the fix is a package update followed by a restart, because upgrading the package does not restart the running sshd: Update the packages: apk upgrade -U -a Restart the server: rc-service sshd restart Point releases 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 already include the fixed package. Branches 3.16 to 3.21 are past their end of support but also got fixed packages. Cloud instances started from tiny-cloud images older than those point releases still need the update, or the setting below. If you build OpenSSH yourself, version 10.6p2 includes the change, as its release notes describe. If you cannot update yet, turning off password logins also stops the attack. First make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until a new login succeeds. Then set PasswordAuthentication no, check the configuration with sshd -t, and restart sshd. The advisory gives commands that add the setting in a drop-in file in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d, which Alpine's default configuration reads from 3.19 onward. They also change every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config from yes to no, including lines inside a Match block. Afterward, sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication should print passwordauthentication no. The advisory suggests looking in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password, such as alpine, root or a key-only user. On exposed machines, also review doas use, recently created users, files and authorized keys. "If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised," it says. Why Long Passwords Work Without PAM, sshd checks a password itself. It hashes the attempt with crypt(), the C library function that turns a password into its stored form, and compares the result with the stored field. An account with no password has only * in that field. That is too short to hold a salt, the random prefix of a hash, so sshd borrows the salt of another account that has a real hash. For the $5$ and $6$ hash types, musl's crypt() refuses passwords longer than 256 bytes and returns * to signal the error. That * matches the stored *, so sshd accepts the login. The upper end of the range is sshd's own limit of 1,024 bytes per password. This behavior comes from a musl change on August 9, 2012, which made a failed crypt() call return "an unmatchable hash rather than NULL" because many programs did not check for failure. The 256-byte limit followed on August 29, 2012, to protect servers from denial-of-service attacks. The salt borrowing comes from a July 15, 2016, OpenSSH change that addressed CVE-2016-6210, a flaw that let attackers learn which usernames exist. Kültekin says the problem has existed since then. The 10.6p2 code change makes sshd refuse a match when the stored field is shorter than four characters. OpenSSH calls it a workaround and says the root cause lies outside sshd. Stable Alpine packages carry a patch for the same problem. Why the Fix Came the Next Day Miller's team learned of the flaw earlier this week and shipped the fix as fast as it could. In the release announcement, he said the team now sees long embargoes as dangerous and mainly helpful to attackers, because it has recently seen AI agents find the same bugs again, sometimes within hours. No CVE identifier had been assigned to the flaw as of today.

e6o6qp.text: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a now-patched vulnerability that could be exploited to bypass Lockdown Mode protections in OpenAI ChatGPT. Lockdown Mode was introduced by the artificial intelligence (AI) company in June 2026 as an optional setting to minimize data exfiltration risks arising from prompt injections. "The flaw could enable silent chat data theft, phishing, and malware delivery, including zero-click data exfiltration in the ChatGPT desktop application," Eli Smadja, head of research at Check Point, said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The problem stems from HTML page previews inside ChatGPT code blocks, which allow HTML content to be rendered directly within the application. Given that executing user-supplied HTML and JavaScript can introduce security risks of its own, the content is placed inside a sandbox so that it cannot access data from the app, such as cookies and local storage. The sandbox also prevents the rendered content from communicating with external resources without user consent. Lockdown Mode acts as a security barrier, mitigating data exfiltration risk by limiting outbound network requests that could be used to transfer sensitive information to an attacker-controlled infrastructure. However, Check Point found a loophole in the manner popup windows are handled during HTML previews that made it possible to escape the confines of the sandbox and bypass Lockdown Mode. "The HTML preview used nested sandboxed frames, and while ChatGPT intercepted direct attempts to open new windows, the underlying sandbox permissions still allowed popups and permitted them to escape the sandbox," Smadja explained. "By creating another nested frame within the rendered page, it was possible to access an unmodified popup function and bypass the restrictions placed on the original HTML preview. Content opened through this route was no longer subject to the same sandbox restrictions, providing a way to circumvent the protections of Lockdown Mode." Once the restrictions are bypassed, a threat actor can exploit the vulnerability to exfiltrate data, chat messages, or deliver malicious payloads by means of a crafted prompt, a malicious GPT, or a shared chat. What's more, as the attacker is in complete control of the content displayed in the popup window, it could be used to render convincing social-engineering lures, such as a fake ChatGPT update, and trick the victim into downloading malware by persuading them to click on a link. That said, the underlying issue is not limited to the Electron-based desktop environment, highlighting how weakness outside of the scope of the AI model can undermine AI security controls. Following responsible disclosure, the vulnerability was addressed by OpenAI on September 18, 2026. "Lockdown Mode was specifically intended to reduce the possibility of data leaving a conversation through potentially malicious outbound requests, yet a weakness in another application feature provided an alternative path around that security boundary," Smadja said. "The finding raises a broader enterprise security issue: AI security controls are only as strong as the wider application environment around them." The disclosure comes a week after Parameter Labs detailed a way to bypass ChatGPT's sandbox and content security policy (CSP) and take over anyone's account simply by sending an attacker-controlled public ChatGPT share link and prompting them to click the HTML preview once. If the HTML block is marked as previewable, it's opened automatically. "An attacker could create a malicious conversation, publish it using ChatGPT's normal sharing feature, and send the link to another user," security researcher Mukul Goyal said. "When the victim opened the share, the payload executed as chatgpt[.]com with access to the victim's authenticated web session." Earlier this September, Check Point also demonstrated a covert cross-account command channel through which an attacker could use a victim's ChatGPT session to run hidden tasks with the tools, data, and connected apps available to that session, alongside the visible conversation. "The victim could receive a normal answer to their visible request while the attacker's task was processed separately and its result returned across accounts," Check Point said. "The channel operated through code-execution environments belonging to different ChatGPT accounts." "The hidden instruction could be delivered through a malicious prompt, a shared ChatGPT conversation, or a custom GPT. Once it was present in the victim's conversation context, an ordinary message could trigger the attacker-controlled task without revealing it in the visible response." The findings coincide with the discovery of a number of security shortcomings in various AI-driven tools and services over the past few months to trick them into spilling secrets or carrying out unauthorized actions - An attack called SkillJacking that hijacks dependencies used by skills (repositories, packages, domains, or cloud apps) to compromise every agent installing them. A set of vulnerabilities in built-in browsers associated with five AI coding assistants, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, OpenAI Codex, Microsoft Visual Studio Code, and Anthropic Claude Desktop that could be exploited to execute code on a host machine, read and steal files, or spoof web browser address bars. The issues have been codenamed Embrace, short for EMbedded BRowser - Arbitrary Code Execution, Arbitrary Content Exfiltration, and Arbitrary Context Emulation. A technique called Repeat-After-Me that targets LangChain LangGraph, Microsoft Agent Framework, Microsoft AutoGen, Google Agent Development Kit 2.0, AWS Strands Agents, and CrewAI and tricks them into running tool calls by means of a "seemingly benign text-repetition request." A vulnerability called AgentCorruption that could allow an attacker to interact with an exposed AI agent running on AWS Bedrock AgentCore and leverage prompt injection techniques to influence that agent and extract its IMDS credentials, and then use them to access other agents, read private conversations, steal connected-tool credentials, and manipulate agent behavior. A vulnerability in SpaceXSI Grok and GitHub Copilot CLI called Cryptographic Context Injection that could be exploited to read a developer's local files and send them to an external server from a single web page via an indirect prompt injection, which hides malicious instructions inside AES-encrypted text. A zero-click vulnerability called SalesBleed that could be exploited to extract sensitive account data out of Salesforce Agentforce by leveraging the Web-to-Lead form to plant an indirect prompt injection payload. A proof-of-concept (PoC) attack called not-a-mused that allows an unprivileged local attacker (or process) to redirect Meta Muse's dictation traffic and abuse the permissions granted to the AI assistant to perform arbitrary actions. A zero-click vulnerability called Plugin4Shell that could be exploited to conduct an AI supply chain attack by silently swapping a trusted plugin with a malicious one while bypassing SHA pinning. "The agent checks out the exact commit the marketplace pinned but never verifies it landed there, so an attacker who controls the plugin's repo makes the checkout resolve to malicious code while the pin still looks honored," Air Security said. "The result is zero-click remote code execution across Claude Code, Codex, GitHub Copilot, and Gemini CLI." An attack called BragJack that can be exploited to hijack the AI agents built into browsers like Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Opera Neon, Perplexity Comet, and Anthropic Claude in Chrome by using an already installed malicious browser extension in conjunction with prompt forcing. A behavioral effect called sampling drift demonstrates how adding an invisible watermark to a large language model's (LLM) output can unintentionally change how the model behaves, including the tools an AI agent invokes, and likely weaken safety refusals. "Watermarking changes refusal behavior on bare harmful requests, but the effect is more pronounced when the same requests are paired with the prompt-injection technique," Lasso Security said. "On several models, watermarking then makes the model more likely to answer harmful requests that it would otherwise refuse." A set of attacks that exploit customer support AI agents to compose and send phishing emails, invoke tool calls, and bypass multi-factor authentication (MFA) protections. A prompt-crafting technique called PuzzleMask that bypasses quick LLM-based policy checks carried out by a lightweight gatekeeper model by planting the malicious instruction in a specially crafted prose wrapper, after which the payload is processed by a more powerful target model to trigger malicious actions. A technique called Workflow Identity Hijacking allows an attacker to bypass standard controls by sending normal, benign requests through an unauthenticated entry point, causing the enterprise AI pipeline to process the request and execute the action as designed. "The core failure is that the requester had no authority to make that request," Noma Security said. "When an AI workflow performs downstream actions, it executes using high-privilege service accounts or developer API keys rather than enforcing the permissions of the external user. As a result, AI workflows become unauthenticated proxies for privileged actions and silent data exfiltration." A zero-click vulnerability class called PleaseFix that could be exploited to hijack AI agents embedded in agentic browsers by placing malicious instructions inside emails, calendar invitations, or web pages, and exploit a technique referred to as intent collision to cause the agent to "act on the attacker's behalf using the user's own identity, permissions and access." A set of vulnerabilities impacting AI coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI that could be exploited to trick them into handing over a victim's secrets, achieving persistent instruction poisoning by modifying the AGENTS.md file, and compromising software releases through prompt injections placed inside untrusted user inputs, like GitHub issues. "Agents are becoming the default infrastructure across CI/CD, messaging, triage, incident response, and support," Novee Security said. "The more autonomous they get, the more the harness decides what's safe on your behalf, and the more untrusted input reaches real execution."

16gqa33.text: How much damage can someone do without breaking much? Quite a lot, it seems. A stolen login can open doors across several systems. A trusted setting can be used to lock people out. Even a simple file copy can reach places it shouldn't. And while new tools are helping find security holes faster, some important systems are still taking months, sometimes over a year, to get patched. Not exactly a great match.The stranger part is how little some attacks now need. Ransom demands without encrypted files. Fake websites that look real enough to steal money. AI tools picking up dangerous instructions while trying to help. Even the attackers are making mistakes in their own code.This week's stories are a reminder that the biggest problems don't always come from clever tricks. Sometimes the easy way works just fine. Here's what else happened.The threats change every week. Subscribe, and we’ll alert you when each new ThreatsDay Bulletin is out. AI Accelerates Zero-Day Discovery The U.K. National Cyber Security Center (NCSC) has warned that the widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has "almost certainly" led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an n-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process," NCSC said. "However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses. Additionally, an organisation’s internal patching and testing processes will need to evolve to meet the pace of accelerating vulnerability discovery. Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal." Critical Systems Face Prolonged Exposure An analysis of roughly 383,000 CVEs disclosed from 1999 through September 2026 has found that the median time to patch a vulnerability exceeds a year for network appliances. About 2,000 CVEs (roughly 0.5%) have been linked to real-world exploitation. "The median vulnerability is patched in about two weeks on Windows workstations but in more than a month on Windows Servers," Microsoft said. "It stretches to 10+ weeks on Linux Servers and for applications running on macOS, and beyond a year on network appliances. That gap is the threat actor's window, widest on the critical systems that stay exposed the longest." The tech giant also said threat actors disproportionately target flaws that maximize impact and exposure and enable system takeover, particularly remote code execution, privilege escalation, and authentication bypass. $4.5 Million Fraud Network Busted Authorities have arrested seven people allegedly involved in an investment fraud scheme that claimed potential victims in more than 50 countries, according to Europol. The operation caused estimated losses of at least $4.5 million. The "crime-as-a-service" offering was run by a company from Cyprus and Israel, and allegedly provided cybercrime groups with an assortment of trading websites and fraudulent call centers tasked with tricking victims into transferring their savings. These call centers operated from Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia. "More than 100 servers were seized and seven suspects arrested during coordinated action on 3 November 2026," Europol said. "Authorities searched 17 locations and seized servers, other evidence and assets." Like other fraudulent investment schemes, the operation leveraged deceptive advertisements to funnel people towards fraudulent investment platforms, promising them substantial, quick returns from cryptocurrency trading and foreign currencies. Although victims were encouraged to transfer a small amount, they displayed illusory gains to push them into transferring increasingly large sums. The operators resorted to delaying tactics to block payments when they attempted to withdraw their funds. "Behind seemingly legitimate platforms, supposed brokers used fictitious profits and sustained psychological pressure to persuade victims to invest more," Europol said. "Personal data collected through this process was sold to criminal groups operating call centers. Operators then contacted potential victims with supposed investment opportunities, turning their initial interest into repeated demands for money." $250K Bounty for Critical Cloud Flaws Google has expanded its Cloud Vulnerability Reward Program (VRP) with a new top-tier reward for high-impact architectural security flaws, allowing researchers to earn $250,000 for Root-in-Cloud bugs, including tenant-isolation bypasses and complex cross-service logic flaws that let attackers gain full administrative control over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations. "To earn this premier reward, you must demonstrate full administrative control, the equivalent of 'roles/owner' or complete IAM control, over arbitrary Google Cloud organizations or projects with no prior access or special project setup," Google said. "Additionally, valid vulnerability reports demonstrating remote code execution (RCE) in underlying Google production infrastructure (Borg) or achieving root-in-prod will automatically be evaluated by the Google Cloud VRP panel for root-in-cloud eligibility." Edge Blocks Scam Notification Abuse Microsoft has announced that its Edge browser will now automatically disable notifications from sites that push scam or scareware notifications, such as fake virus warnings or security alerts. "As of last month’s rollout of Edge 156, when Microsoft Defender SmartScreen or Scareware blocker detects a scam that was pushed through a notification, Edge will automatically disable notifications from the site that sent it," Microsoft said. "The next time Edge starts, an information bar explains what happened. If you believe a site was blocked incorrectly, you can review sites with blocked notifications and unblock them from Edge Settings, keeping you in control." University Cryptojacking Charges Two Canadian men, Ryan James Roach, 35, and Mathiew James Stubbings, 41, have been indicted in the U.S. for hacking multiple U.S. universities and using the access to mine cryptocurrency. Both have been charged with conspiracy to obtain information from a protected computer and to cause damage to a protected computer, obtaining information from a protected computer, and intentional damage to a protected computer, which carry a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison and a $250,000 fine. "Between June 2016, and December 2019, Roach and Stubbings conspired to engage in a scheme to hack into computers, steal login credentials, and secretly mine cryptocurrency for financial gain," the Justice Department said. "They used virtual private servers in multiple countries, which were registered under false names. These servers transmitted malware and mining software to victim computers and stored stolen login credentials. Victims of the scheme included educational institutions in New York, Tennessee, North Carolina, and Massachusetts." Ransomware Extortion Without Encryption Cybersecurity researchers have detailed an encryptionless extortion attack involving PAYLOAD ransomware targeting a manufacturing organization in the Middle East. "The threat actor obtained domain admin-equivalent control of the organization’s Active Directory environment and authored a malicious Group Policy Object (GPO) named PAYLOAD, linking it at the domain root," Kaspersky said. "Through that single object, the actor delivered ransom notes, hijacked the desktop wallpaper and lock screen, enforced a logon banner, and disabled the local administrator account across every domain-joined Windows workstation — all without dropping a ransomware binary or encrypting any data. The only ransomware we found in this incident was a PAYLOAD sample targeting ESXi on Linux servers." The attack represents a convergence of two trends: Living-off-the-land abuse of trusted AD infrastructure and a surge in extortion-only incidents. AI Sandbox Escape Exposes Sensitive Files A vulnerability impacting Docker Sandboxes (CVE-2026-103916) could have been exploited to bypass file access restrictions, potentially exposing cloud credentials and other sensitive files on a developer's machine through a routine copy command. "The command used to copy files between a sandbox and the developer's computer (sbx cp) does not enforce these access restrictions," Endor Labs said. "An agent can exploit this weakness using what is known as a symbolic link, essentially a shortcut that points to another file or folder. By placing a malicious shortcut inside an approved workspace, the agent can trick a subsequent copy command into accessing files outside the sandbox's approved boundaries." The issue has been addressed in Docker Sandboxes version 0.51.0. Smart TVs Keep Tracking After Opt-OutDoes Opting Out of ACR Work? A new study has revealed that smart TVs running operating systems from Samsung, Vizio, and Roku continue to transmit data to automatic content recognition (ACR) endpoints even after users opt out of tracking in the devices' settings. "Opting out fully worked on only four operating systems. On Samsung and Vizio, traffic consistent with ACR kept flowing, and Roku's opt-out doesn't cover its own streaming service," according to a group of academics from Northeastern University. "VIDAA OS sends ACR data to servers run by Unruly over MQTT without encryption, so anyone on the network path between the TV and those servers can read it." Cryptographic Proof for AI Outputs Anthropic has revealed that it's working on an open-source system called FlashProve to cryptographically verify an AI response came from a given model. "FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models," Anthropic said. "FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the prover) and a user (the verifier). It is split into two phases: In the offline phase, the prover publishes a commitment to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down one exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase. In the online phase, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement: The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated. Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens." FTP and Webmail Credentials Exposed DreamHost has warned of a data breach after an unauthorized third party gained access to the server that runs its web-based File Manager at files.dreamhost.com between August and October 23, 2026. "The unauthorized third party exploited a vulnerability in that software and was able to access the FTP/SFTP usernames and passwords of individuals who logged into this File Manager between approximately August 2026 and October 23, 2026," the company said. "The unauthorized third party was also able to reach certain webmail systems, which may have exposed the session information (the data that keeps a user signed in, including session credentials) of a limited number of webmail users. We believe this was a deliberate attack, and our team worked around the clock to contain it." DreamHost said the attacker may have accessed the credentials used to access the File Manager or webmail, along with the contents of emails and files in the FTP/SFTP server. There is no evidence that the attacker accessed control panel login information or customer billing details. Pre-Auth RCE and Account Takeover The maintainers of Apache OFBiz have addressed 46 security flaws, including CVE-2026-68524, which could result in pre-authentication remote code execution, and CVE-2026-109928, which enables full account takeover due to an incorrect authentication algorithm implementation. The issues have been patched in Apache OFBiz 24.09.08. Ransomware Encryption Flaws Exposed Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered encryption weaknesses in the updated HYFLOCK ransomware builds. The ransomware operation began to publicly name victims in October 2026, although evidence indicates that the group first appeared in underground forums in March 2026. As of writing, the group has listed 13 victims. "The October 17 build successfully encrypted files, registered a scheduled task, accessed network-share resources, and attempted to interfere with system recovery," Check Point said. "In an earlier October version, researchers identified a processing defect that could permanently discard portions of a file, potentially preventing complete recovery even with the correct decryption key. The October 17 build exhibited another issue. Larger files had only their first 4,096 bytes encrypted, leaving additional content accessible beyond that initial section." Customer Identity Data Accessed DigiCert said it has identified an event involving unauthorized access to one of its business systems that stores information shared by customer representatives to validate their identity. The company said its certificate operations were not impacted. "Most of the data was limited to business contact information for customers: names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses," DigiCert said. "A small minority of customer accounts included additional personal data in the form of a customer-provided document such as a driver's license, passport, utility bill, or other document with name and address. The access could not write records, act as a validation approver, or issue certificates." DeFi Hijack Drains $138K Threat actors have hijacked a little over a dozen DeFi websites registered with Name.com, including Flap, Kintsu, Pickle Finance and Origami Finance, ultimately stealing about $138,000 in assets. The sites have been found to be rigged with a malware kit that tricks visitors into approving transfers out of their wallets once they connect them to the compromised site. Vercel said it's aware of nine domains associated with the platform that were impacted. "Over about 45 minutes on Oct 31 (UTC), an account within an associated support team made changes to the nameservers associated with 15 domains registered with name.com," Name.com said in a post-mortem. "The domains were directed to a malicious page hosting Step Drainer malware." Stolen Cloud App Credentials Abused Todyl has disclosed that an unknown threat actor has been abusing stolen Microsoft Entra ID application credentials and Azure DevOps identities to access MSPs' Microsoft 365 and Azure environments, reaching at least 27 organizations. "About 45 app registrations at roughly 18 organizations were targeted, and more than 33 of them authenticated successfully," Todyl said. "Through those apps the actor has reached 27 organizations so far, including the MSPs' downstream clients in government, energy, food and agriculture, transportation, construction and engineering, legal, education and nonprofits. It has run searches across about 25 tenants, downloaded 81 files and accessed around 2,279 mailbox items." The sign-in activity has originated from the IP address 199.19.77[.]84. Syrian Hacker Gets 42 Months Ahmad Umar Agha (aka Th3Pr0), a Syrian national tied to the Syrian Electronic Army (SEA), has been sentenced to 42 months in prison in the U.S. for his involvement in an expansive hacking conspiracy organized and led by members of former Syrian President Bashar Al-Assad regime between Aug 2011 and January 2014. "To spread the former Syrian government's propaganda, Agha hacked approximately 47 Western media entities, businesses, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and U.S. and allied government entities," the Justice Department said. "In one instance, Agha’s actions caused a flash crash in the U.S. stock market, resulting in a temporary $136 billion loss in the value of stocks making up the Dow Jones Industrial Average." Agha and his alleged accomplice, Firas Dardar, were first charged in June 2014. Dardar remains at large. Malicious AI Search Results Steal Crypto A new piece of malware has been observed targeting AI agents creating cryptocurrency wallets. "A GitHub repository posing as a Solana starter kit, which ranks as the top result when an agent searches for one, contains malware that gives an attacker remote control of the victim's machine, including the crypto wallets on it," AIR Security said. The activity has been codenamed SolanaCry. The attack builds upon the foundation of Web Hole, where an AI agent, in its quest for finding answers to a problem, can inadvertently run a command suggested by an attacker and perform malicious actions. "To get a payload into search results, an attacker has two options," AIR said. "The first is to build a site of their own and grow its reputation with SEO, backlinks, content, time, until the search engine treats it as relevant and trusted. Once it ranks, they change the content and drop in the payload. The second is easier: find dead sites that still show up as ranked results, and use those to deliver it." Android Banking Malware Spreads Thousands of Android phones belonging to retail banking customers in the Middle East, Turkey, and Africa (META) region have been compromised with the Mirax trojan between March and September 2026, leading to estimated losses worth millions of U.S. dollars. "Where unauthorized international transfers were reported, funds were sent to accounts abroad, some of which are suspected to be mule accounts," Group-IB said. "The campaign uses dynamically generated package names and impersonates 'Google Play Services' to evade user suspicion and signature-based detection." Like most Android malware, Mirax is used to facilitate device takeover (DTO) fraud by abusing Android's accessibility services. "With it, the attacker is able to see and control the compromised device in real time: reading credentials, intercepting one-time codes, capturing the PIN to unlock the device later, opening a banking app and moving money out to newly added beneficiaries and mule accounts abroad," Group-IB said. Campaigns using Mirax have been attributed to Aquafina, a threat actor known to be active since March 16, 2026. AI Model Bypasses Task Instructions Irregular's evaluation of Zhipu AI's open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench has found that the model "did not refuse any of the tested offensive tasks" and "repeatedly reached correct answers while violating explicit task instructions." The AI security company said these violations can be interpreted as a form of reward hacking. "Crediting the answer alone could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions, while rewarding it during training could reinforce these instruction violations," it added. One thing stands out this week: attackers don't always need to be smarter than the systems they're targeting. They just need to find what was missed, left open, or trusted a little too much. And with AI making some of that searching easier, the time between finding a problem and using it is getting shorter. Patching still matters, but so does checking whether the controls already in place actually work.That's it for this week. Some of these problems have fixes. Others need a closer look at how people, tools, and systems are allowed to work together. The next big headache may not come from a new bug at all. It could be something that's been sitting there for years, waiting for someone to notice. See you next week.

ukl4g1.text: A critical finding can move through several security tools and still leave the organization exposed. The vulnerability has a severity score, and a ticket has reached the queue. Progress then depends on information the finding may lack: who owns the system, whether attackers can reach it, what protection exists, and how a change could affect the business. Each missing detail creates another investigation, another handoff, and another delay. An exposure management platform should connect discovery with a clear priority, an appropriate response, and evidence that protection has improved. Continuous threat exposure management (CTEM) connects this work through scoping, discovery, prioritization, validation, and mobilization. These five tests establish whether a platform can support that process across infrastructure, identities, sensitive data, and external threats. Security teams often have several records of the same asset. A cloud platform identifies an instance, an endpoint tool records its hostname, and an inventory lists an owner who has changed roles. Cyber asset attack surface management (CAASM) connects those records, helping reveal stale information, missing ownership, and protection gaps. The resulting view needs enough detail to support action: the asset’s owner, business purpose, assessment history, and security coverage. A system with no reported vulnerabilities should be distinguishable from one never assessed. Disagreements between sources also need to remain visible. If an endpoint tool reports an active server while the inventory marks it retired, source records and update times help teams resolve the conflict. Figure 1. CAASM connects source records with asset ownership, security coverage, and exposure context. External discovery adds another perspective. External attack surface management (EASM) helps uncover what assets make accessible from the outside, including shadow IT, forgotten subdomains, and exposed services that internal tools never see. EASM and CAASM work best together: CAASM maps what you know you own, while EASM validates that picture from the attacker’s point of view and surfaces what’s missing. Every unmanaged asset EASM finds can be fed back into CAASM, closing coverage gaps and giving each asset an owner. EASM also covers brand exposure, extending discovery to phishing sites, fraudulent profiles, and brand impersonation, so the same external view that finds your unknown assets also finds the lookalikes attackers build to target your customers and employees. Read CAASM Was Never Meant to Stand Alone to see how asset intelligence supports the decisions and actions that follow discovery. 2. Explain Which Exposures Require Action First Prioritization depends on understanding what an exposure actually puts at risk. A customer-facing application may carry the same severity score as an isolated development system while presenting very different business risk. Prioritization should connect: Reachability and exploitability: Whether attackers have a usable path to exploit the weakness. Threat activity: Whether attackers are targeting the vulnerability or technology. Business impact: What the system supports and what compromise could affect. Existing protection: Whether relevant controls cover the system and are enforced. Those conditions change. New exploitation activity may accelerate a response, while a disabled protection may invalidate an earlier assessment. External threats need similarly specific reasoning. A fraudulent support account approaching customers may require rapid disruption; an abandoned company profile may first need ownership review. See what the 2026 Exposure Gap Report reveals about prioritization and remediation performance. 3. Validate the Exposure and the Proposed Response A clear priority can still stall when the system owner lacks confidence in the proposed change. Validation needs to establish what the exposure allows and how the response could affect operations. Identifying vulnerable software, confirming reachability, and demonstrating exploitability establish different things. A platform should distinguish observed evidence from analysis and untested assumptions. Attack-path relationships also need supporting evidence and clear limitations. The proposed response requires separate assessment. A patch may depend on application testing and a maintenance window. An intrusion prevention system protection may require observation in Detect mode before enforcement. Evidence should address the action’s scope, dependencies, false positives, performance impact, and recovery options. Following a proposed change through this assessment reveals what the platform establishes and what teams must investigate themselves. 4. Carry Safe Remediation Through Existing Workflows Knowing what to fix first is great, but only if the fix happens quickly. The permanent patch often waits on testing, approval, and a maintenance window, and the exposure stays open the whole time. That’s true whether the weakness is on an internet-facing server or a phishing site targeting your customers. Speed comes from confidence. Teams hesitate when they can’t say what an action will touch. When the platform already knows the asset, its owner, the active threat, and the controls in place, that hesitation disappears. Many Check Point Exposure Management customers remediate safely within one hour, because the context is complete and the safety checks are built in. To test this, take one real finding and follow it from priority to protection: Owner: Is the right person assigned automatically? Safety: Is the action validated before it runs, including its impact and a way back? Execution: Does it run through the controls you already have, whether a virtual patch, a configuration change, or a takedown? Confirmation: Is the result verified, with the permanent fix still tracked? Interim protection buys time, but it shouldn’t replace the long term fix. Figure 2. Safe remediation connects observation, validation, action, and confirmation. Speed holds up at scale. Between January 1 and October 26, 2026, an airline group completed more than 1,500 takedowns of profiles impersonating its airlines and support teams, combining analyst review with automated remediation. And when an action fails, the exposure should stay visible with a clear next step. Read Safe Remediation: Confident Remediation in Production to see how validation, execution, and confirmation work together. 5. Show What Changed and What Remains A completed action needs evidence of the resulting state. A patch may miss unavailable systems. A policy update may exclude an intended asset. A takedown request may be accepted before the account disappears. Verification should establish whether the vulnerability remains, protection is enforced, or malicious content has been removed. Monitoring should identify recurrence. Reporting must distinguish removed vulnerabilities, interim mitigations, completed takedowns, and accepted risk. Each leaves different responsibilities outstanding. Mean time to remediate (MTTR) requires agreed starting points, completion criteria, and treatment of temporary protection. Tracking assignment, approval, execution, and verification separately reveals delays. Recurring findings, failed actions, and aging mitigations can expose operational problems another scan will not resolve. Apply the Tests Across Vendors Platforms approach these requirements from different foundations. The five tests provide a consistent basis for evaluating coverage, evidence, and action. Check Point Exposure Management combines internal asset intelligence, external discovery, threat intelligence, and brand protection with prioritization, exploitability validation, and safe remediation. It spans infrastructure weaknesses, phishing, and brand impersonation, supporting action through existing controls and takedown workflows. Bring Intelligence Through to Safe Action The five tests follow an exposure from discovery to a confirmed response. Each stage should give the next team enough reliable information to act while keeping unresolved work visible. Check Point Exposure Management carries asset and threat context into responses to vulnerabilities, control gaps, and external threats. Proposed actions are evaluated before enforcement, with approved responses coordinated through supported Check Point and third-party technologies. That connection helps organizations strengthen protection while accounting for production constraints and building on existing investments. It creates a traceable path from an identified exposure to an evaluated, implemented, and confirmed response. 25d7it.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 05, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Vulnerability OpenAI on Wednesday detailed a pipeline that employed an upcoming cyber-focused artificial intelligence (AI) model to validate and patch 948 local privilege escalation vulnerabilities in Linux for $1.2 million in API costs. "Our prototype identified and analyzed 2,308 candidate Linux kernel findings, dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities, and produced 948 local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits that could allow an unprivileged local user to gain root access," the AI company said. The findings build upon 24 LPE exploits that OpenAI revealed were discovered by its GPT‑5.5‑Cyber model back in June 2026. The latest research turns this process into an agentic pipeline comprising five stages - Vulnerability discovery, where agents identify high-value audit targets (i.e., parts of the codebase that are security-relevant and reachable by low-privileged users) and look for candidate findings Dynamic validation, where agents attempt to reproduce each candidate in a sandboxed environment and preserve runtime evidence Exploitability assessment, where agents test whether validated vulnerabilities could be abused to facilitate information disclosure or LPE and devise a proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit Patch generation, where agents generate patches for the identified vulnerability Human review, where security researchers review the exploit, patch, and proposed severity before it's reported to the maintainers "In a run in mid-October 2026, our pipeline using an upcoming cyber model dynamically reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities [within 30 hours] and generated PoCs for 291 information leak vulnerabilities and 948 working local privilege escalation (LPE) exploits for a commonly used Linux distribution," OpenAI said. "The total run cost $1,213,430 in API credits, or $1,279 per LPE exploit. To the best of our knowledge, the agents in this pipeline discovered and used at least 10 novel Linux exploitation techniques." At a high level, these include - Two new persistent elastic objects to spray objects inside the target kernel cache Two new page grooming techniques to improve exploit reliability Five new data-only techniques to obtain privilege escalation directly or via an arbitrary write One technique that involves arbitrary type confusion The development is once again an indication of how frontier AI is redrawing the contours of cybersecurity, accelerating vulnerability discovery and exploitation, and at the same time helping defenders reliably address defects, albeit through additional instructions and iterations, before attackers can use them, and make it "cost prohibitive" for bad actors to exploit software. In a report published last month, VulnCheck categorized AI-assisted vulnerability discovery as a "growing risk category" that turbocharges novice hackers, who now require little to no technical expertise to detect software vulnerabilities. The access to AI models is not just limited to defenders, but also bad actors who can leverage the same capabilities to discover and weaponize new zero-days and expand the pool of viable targets with minimal effort. According to insights from Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), the number of vulnerabilities disclosed per month has more than doubled, rising from 5,045 in January 2026 to 10,740 in August 2026. The number of vulnerabilities classified as high-risk has surged from 131 disclosures in January 2026 to 350 in August 2026, a 167% growth. "The widespread availability of AI-powered cyber tools has almost certainly led to a significant increase in the discovery of zero-day vulnerabilities," the U.K. National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) said in an assessment published Tuesday. "Defensive AI-cyber tools have reduced the window of a vulnerability moving from zero-day to an N-day vulnerability, and have made patching a quicker process. However, without correct and widespread configuring of this technology, many systems are still vulnerable to attackers using AI-cyber tools to identify and exploit system weaknesses." The NCSC also pointed out that organizations will have to evolve their internal patching and testing processes to meet this new pace of vulnerability discovery. "Attackers have subsequently displayed less caution over losing an access to achieve an objective, as the cost to replace is minimal," it added. "Cyber capabilities are now used for a broader range of activity due to the lower risk involved, making it easier for adversaries to access information and use it operationally." OpenAI said the rate of vulnerability discovery by frontier models needs to be matched by automated patch generation to secure software and to limit the exploitation window. "With human expert-guided iteration, we believe AI-generated patches can be functionally correct, aligned with existing coding styles, and robust to attack variants," OpenAI said. "For the near and medium term, having access to a low-privileged account on an operating system that isn't up-to-date on its latest available patches should be considered functionally equivalent to root access for a well-resourced threat actor."

vkwz11.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 05, 2026Cloud Security / Data Privacy Apple has revealed that it plans to start checking public iCloud links for harmful content starting with iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and visionOS 27.3. The change specifically applies to scenarios where users share iCloud content, such as photos in iCloud Photos or files in iCloud Drive, by sharing a link and making it accessible to "Anyone with the link." When users choose this option, it makes the content accessible to anyone who has the link, including Apple, the iPhone maker said. "Starting in version 27.3 or later of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, and visionOS, items shared using Anyone with the Link will be checked by Apple for harmful content," it said in a support document published Tuesday. Apple also explicitly noted that sharing an item that can be accessed by Anyone with the Link disables end-to-end encryption (E2EE), even if the owner or the recipients have turned on Advanced Data Protection, an optional setting that secures iCloud Backup, Photos, and Notes using E2EE. That said, it's unclear what prompted this change, what Apple considers as "harmful content," and whether these checks will also be applied retroactively to previously generated links, as well as any new links created before the 27.3 updates are officially rolled out later this December. The tech giant has also warned that if users attempt to upload harmful content, it can be removed or deleted at any time. "Apple may also take action against your Apple Account, including blocking or disabling your Apple Account, blocking the ability to create a new Apple Account with the associated email address or phone number, or if necessary, involving law enforcement," it said.

8vudt0.text: The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) has disclosed that an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted threat actor it tracks as Crafty Falcon is targeting organizations in the Banking, Financial Services, and Insurance (BFSI) sectors in the country. Describing the threat as active and ongoing, the activity involves the use of publicly-available AI-driven offensive security tools like ARTEX, PentAGI, Cairn, and CyberStrikeAI. "These tools execute complete attack chains autonomously at machine speed, generate and refine large numbers of tailored attack scripts in rapid succession, and adapt their payloads based on target responses," CERT-In said. "The supporting attack infrastructure rotates IP addresses within hours to days." The agency said the attacks have also targeted cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset service providers, resulting in the theft of keys and funds. The update follows an October 2026 alert issued by CERT-In, which warned of multiple cyber attack campaigns targeting non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), digital lending platforms, fintech entities, payment service providers, and cryptocurrency wallet operators. Threat actors have been observed exploiting internet-facing applications and exposed APIs and privileged endpoints to steal payment aggregator/gateway and partner-bank API credentials, and then invoke fund-transfer APIs directly from within the entities' own allow-listed infrastructure. Some of the other notable initial access vectors are listed below - Use of stolen long-lived static, hard-coded API tokens Supply chain compromise of source code repositories via forged commits Exploitation of plaintext credentials in configuration files, source code, or databases Access to applications and remote services lacking multi-factor authentication (MFA) This approach, CERT-In added, defeats application-level controls such as loan creation, KYC, sanction, beneficiary verification, balance sufficiency, and per-transaction limits. The rapidly executed fraudulent transactions are designed to move funds to attacker-controlled mule accounts across multiple banks. In addition, the attacks involve the operators taking steps to delete logs and tamper with endpoint security tools in an attempt to complicate detection and incident response efforts. CERT-In also warned that attackers are targeting cloud infrastructure to execute commands and deploy malicious payloads, as well as publicly-accessible non-production environments to obtain shared credentials, tokens, or network paths, and then use them to pivot to production systems. Other notable post-exploitation actions undertaken by the adversary are as follows - Reverse-engineering application codebases to develop tailored exploits Initiating unauthorized API calls using modified application packages, undermining controls that "assumed only the legitimate client application would call the APIs" Executing micro-value test transactions (such as Rs. 1) to validate unauthorized fund flows before executing large-value transfers Abusing merchant settlement APIs of payment aggregators to move funds Exploiting newly disclosed vulnerabilities, including file-upload and deserialization exploit chains leading to web shells in PHP and Node.js applications Creating a large number of custom scripts on the fly and iteratively improving them in quick succession, a pattern consistent with AI-assisted development The development comes as CERT-In has published the Artificial Intelligence Security Auditing Guidelines, laying out specific requirements to ensure the "governance, security, privacy, fairness, transparency, resilience and auditability of AI systems." The framework calls for testing an AI agent's documented identities, authorized objectives, approved tool use, permission boundaries, and its adherence to the principle of least privilege (PoLP). It also requires AI agents to require human approval for consequential actions, while ensuring high-risk AI systems incorporate emergency interruption, credential revocation, and controls for preventing automatic restarts. "Effective assurance requires organisational accountability, technical testing, data and model governance, continuous monitoring, human oversight, incident response and third-party assurance," the agency said. "Accordingly, the framework provides auditable requirements proportionate to the nature, scale, autonomy and potential impact of each AI system." Copycat ARTEX Version Hands Out Root Shell The abuse of open-source penetration testing tools like ARTEX in real-world intrusions prompted its developer to take down the repository from GitHub. But multiple copies have sprung up on the Microsoft-owned code-hosting platform to fill the void - github[.]com/trhhubsd/ARTEXX github[.]com/mhtsec/ARTEX ("mianhuatang11/artex" on Docker Hub) github[.]com/RuoJi6/ARTEX The first two GitHub repositories are no longer available for download. According to an independent cybersecurity researcher who goes by the online alias Badbyte, the "trhhubsd/ARTEX" repository was starred 2,449 times and forked over 600 times. What's notable about the GitHub copy is that it changed a single line in "docker-compose.yml" to pull the "tomicdd/artex" image from Docker Hub. The modified version conceals a new routine that grants a root shell during an unauthenticated request to the login endpoint. Per statistics shared by Docker Hub, the image has been downloaded 9,000 times. "It adds a hidden verifyCaptcha() function to the login handler: if the CAPTCHA field starts with a secret marker, the rest runs through sh -c as root and the output is returned, before any credential check," the researcher said in a statement shared with The Hacker News via email. "That's an unauthenticated root shell on every install, and it never shows up in a code review." "A compromised ARTEX instance holds its targets' unpatched findings, live credentials, captured sessions and network position. Whoever holds the backdoor can also quietly change what the agents do on the next run." As many as 62 ARTEX consoles on the internet have been found to serve the backdoored build between November 2 and 4, 2026, with the first instance going up by October 20, 2026, twelve days after the Docker image was pushed. Of these, 26 consoles are located in the U.S., followed by 17 in Hong Kong and seven in China. In all, a total of 1,645 hosts have been found serving the ARTEX console as of November 4, 2026. Besides "tomicdd/artex," a number of Docker Hub namespaces have been identified as publishing images named "artex." Some of them are listed below - congdonglinux/artex (also backdoored and identical to "tomicdd/artex") mianhuatang11/artex autumn26/artex andy1099zz/artex dgddw/artex trhhubsd/ARTEX ylh440104/artex "The backdoor's author needed nothing more. The people they were after had already chosen to run an unvetted attack tool as root on an open port," Badbyte said. "We know ARTEX has been used maliciously in the wild, and it will keep being used that way. We also know that plenty of legitimate, curious people installed it to see what the fuss was about. They did not sign up for a root shell on their own server."

jzkb7k.text: Zyxel GS1900 network switches that received the vendor's earlier fix for an actively exploited flaw are still open to the exploit attackers used, researchers at Binarly found. The exploit lets anyone who can reach a switch's web management interface run commands on it without logging in. Zyxel has released new firmware for 10 GS1900 models that closes the hole. The earlier fix is the 2.90 Patch 2 firmware, named in a June 16 advisory for a flaw tracked as CVE-2026-7273. The new 2.90 Patch 3 firmware fixes a flaw now tracked separately as CVE-2026-107441, which the exploit relies on. It was posted on October 23, and the vendor announced it in an advisory earlier this week. The researchers, who reported the flaw to the vendor on September 29, call it a zero-day. Attackers already had a working exploit for it by then. GreyNoise, which monitors attack traffic through a network of sensors, reported on September 21 that attackers took data from 996 GS1900 switches around August 17. It tied the attacks to CVE-2026-7273, and the researchers say the exploit it described matches the one they found. Neither GreyNoise nor Binarly says the attacked switches were running the earlier fix, and the vendor's advisory does not say whether the new flaw has been exploited. Which Switches Need the New Firmware Zyxel's security advisory lists the affected and fixed firmware for each model: Model Affected firmware Fixed firmware GS1900-8 2.90(AAHH.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHH.3)C0 GS1900-8HP 2.90(AAHI.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHI.3)C0 GS1900-10HP 2.90(AAZI.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAZI.3)C0 GS1900-16 2.90(AAHJ.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHJ.3)C0 GS1900-24 2.90(AAHL.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHL.3)C0 GS1900-24E 2.90(AAHK.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHK.3)C0 GS1900-24EP 2.90(ABTO.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(ABTO.3)C0 GS1900-24HPv2 2.90(ABTP.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(ABTP.3)C0 GS1900-48 2.90(AAHN.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(AAHN.3)C0 GS1900-48HPv2 2.90(ABTQ.2)C0 and earlier 2.90(ABTQ.3)C0 Switches on Patch 2 or any earlier firmware need the Patch 3 build for their model. The builds are posted with their firmware release notes. The advisory lists no workaround for owners who cannot update yet. It also does not say whether updating removes access an attacker may already have, or what owners should check if a switch may have been compromised. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-7273 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on September 21 and gave federal agencies until September 24 to apply the vendor's fix, the Patch 2 firmware. The listing came the day the earlier attacks were made public. The researchers' vulnerability advisory says the new flaw is present in all 10 of those Patch 2 builds. It also says "an attacker only needs network reachability to the management service", while the vendor's advisory describes a "LAN-based, unauthenticated attacker". The researchers rate the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS severity scale, against 8.8 in the vendor's CVE entry, and say the attacker's commands run with root privileges. Why the Earlier Fix Did Not Stop the Exploit Binarly's technical analysis traces the flaw to the program that handles web requests on the switch. It is an out-of-bounds write, meaning the program writes data beyond the memory allocated for it. The program stores each request parameter in a fixed area that can accommodate 140 parameters. It never checked the size of a parameter, and before Patch 2 it never checked how many parameters it had stored. The exploit sends a 140th parameter that is too large, causing it to overrun the end of that area and overwrite the program's parameter counter. The next parameter is then written outside the area, allowing the attacker to swap the function the program is about to call for one that runs the attacker's command. Patch 2 added a check on the counter, but the check runs only after the oversized parameter has been copied. By then the counter holds the attacker's value, so the check does not stop the write. The researchers say the exploit works against Patch 2 without changes. They tested it on emulated firmware and on real hardware, though they do not say which model. The exploit's own list of supported firmware includes the Patch 2 build for the GS1900-24. According to the researchers, Zyxel told them that CVE-2026-7273 was about the missing counter check, and that it treats the missing size check as a separate flaw, now CVE-2026-107441. In the Patch 3 code, the counter is checked before a parameter is copied, and the copy is limited in size. The researchers say this fixes the flaw. What Is Known About the Attacks GreyNoise's attack report says the attackers used the exploit to download a data-collection script onto the switches and left the collected data to be picked up. The data included switch configurations, hashed root credentials, and network information. Of the 996 switches, 564 still used factory-default credentials. The report does not say which firmware the switches were running or how the attackers reached them. It says the attackers are the same as, or related to, a group that Acronis tracks as Red Heron and describes as Chinese-speaking. Acronis linked a backdoor called JITTERLY to Red Heron in an earlier campaign that targeted Gitea servers. The researchers found the exploit on September 17 in an open folder on a server that also acted as a command server for JITTERLY. Their advisory offers two explanations. Either the Patch 2 update was a faulty fix for CVE-2026-7273, or the attacks exploited a different flaw from the one CISA listed. The researchers say they will soon publish a smaller version of the exploit as a proof of concept. CISA's KEV catalog data, last updated yesterday, does not list CVE-2026-107441.

6lmlfu.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Linux / Vulnerability A flaw in APT, the package manager for Debian and Ubuntu, allows an attacker who can modify package downloads to swap a checked package for their own. The attacker's code then runs as root, according to advisories that Debian, Ubuntu, and APT's developers published on November 4. The attack needs APT to retry failed downloads, which it does by default from Debian 12 and Ubuntu 22.04 onward. Debian has released fixed versions of APT for the flaw, CVE-2026-109518. APT's developers, who call the flaw critical, say updates for Ubuntu and its Ubuntu Pro subscription service are being released. Ubuntu 14.04 users with Ubuntu Pro can already get one. Older releases, such as Debian 11 and Ubuntu 20.04, are not exposed by default, according to Ubuntu. But many user scripts may have turned on the retry setting, Acquire::Retries, on those releases anyway, APT's developers say. Debian's testing branch was still on the vulnerable version 3.3.5 at 14:58 UTC on November 4. For Debian 11, whose Debian long-term support ended on August 31, APT's developers have published a fixed version, 2.2.5. Ubuntu rates the flaw as high priority, with a CVSS 4.0 score of 7.7, and says that distributions built on Debian and Ubuntu are affected as well, without naming any. Ubuntu published new APT builds for four of its releases to its security archive at 14:25 UTC on November 4: Ubuntu 26.10: 3.3.3ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 26.04 LTS: 3.2.1ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 24.04 LTS: 2.8.4ubuntu0.1 Ubuntu 22.04 LTS: 2.4.15ubuntu0.1 At 15:46 UTC, Ubuntu still marked all eight releases it tracks for the flaw, from 14.04 LTS to 26.10, as vulnerable. The attacker can be anyone who can change the HTTP traffic between APT and the package server, including a malicious mirror or proxy, according to Ubuntu. The attack runs when the computer installs a package. The attacker uses HTTP redirects and ordinary temporary server errors to make APT retry the download, APT's developers say. Max Justicz reported the flaw. None of the three advisory reports describe attacks exploiting the flaw or offer a workaround for systems that cannot update yet. They describe the attack over HTTP and do not say whether package sources reached over HTTPS are exposed.

19v5obf.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 04, 2026Artificial Intelligence / Cybersecurity Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of an OpenAI Codex jailbreak bundle that's designed to modify an artificial intelligence (AI) agent's trusted instructions to insert advertisements for a third-party AI gateway. The phenomenon has been codenamed prompt adware by Check Point Research. Called Haiou (meaning Seagull in Chinese), the jailbreak modifies OpenAI Codex's configuration files to inject advertisements for the jailbreak author's website into subsequent agent responses. "The advertised service is an opaque, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway, a middleware between an application and an LLM provider," Check Point Research said in a technical report. "The likely business model is to use the freely distributed jailbreak bundle as an acquisition channel for the paid gateway service." Adware is a type of software that displays unwanted advertisements, which can appear on users' computers or mobile devices, often in the form of pop-ups or banners. Prompt adware extends this sketchy behavior to AI agents by means of a jailbreak that defeats the model's safety training and content guardrails. The idea is to persistently modify the agent's global instructions through natural language to influence future responses. This, in turn, causes common greetings or activation words like "Seagull," "hi," "hello," "hey," "yo," and "are you there?" to trigger an advertisement for "zz.aiapi2025[.]top." Haiou attempts to jailbreak a model by using several prompt injection techniques, such as role-playing and reframing cybersecurity-related requests into a Capture The Flag (CTF) scenario. In addition, it installs security-focused skills devoted to penetration testing, cracking, and reverse engineering. However, it doesn't stop there. The bundle also injects persistent ads into the global agent instruction file to promote the LLM gateway website. On GitHub, "haiou-codex" is advertised as a "local enhancement configuration package" that adds a "Chinese technical personality and security research workflow to Codex." As of writing, the repository has been forked 77 times and starred 403 times since it was made available on July 10, 2026. It's worth noting that Codex is not officially available in mainland China, suggesting that the service is likely aimed at individuals or organizations wanting to try out Western AI coding assistants. What's more, the jailbreak has been bundled within Codex-X, an open-source Chinese visualization tool for configuring Codex through a graphical user interface. "The behavior is introduced through natural-language instructions and configuration, rather than a traditional executable payload that users and security teams may more readily recognize as software behavior," Pedro Drimel Neto, malware analysis team leader at Check Point, said. While serving an ad may seem relatively harmless in the larger scheme of things, the findings demonstrate how a bad actor could introduce undesirable behavior through third-party skills or configurations, leading to supply chain attacks. "As AI agents become part of enterprise environments, the prompts, Skills and third-party components influencing their behavior become part of the trust chain too," Neto said.

j6tadl.text: The Russia-linked threat actor known as APT29 is said to be behind a large-scale watering hole campaign targeting iOS and Android users through compromised websites, fake domains, and a supply chain attack involving a Ukrainian web analytics service called Plerdy SEO Tracker. "The injected JavaScript code collects browser and device attributes," Sekoia researchers Amaury-Jacques Garçon and Félix Aime said in a technical report shared with The Hacker News. "Then, the delivery infrastructure delivers a platform-specific N-day exploit chain targeting either iOS or Android." The end goal of the attacks is to serve payloads capable of stealing browser cookies, and in some cases, Wi-Fi passwords or full mobile device data. The activity, codenamed Poisoned Source, was discovered by the French cybersecurity company in mid-October 2026. A defining aspect of the campaign is the use of three infection vectors - Compromise of legitimate websites to inject malicious JavaScript Lookalike sites masquerading as high-profile websites in the U.S. ("america250[.]holiday"), Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Bulgaria Supply chain compromise of Plerdy SEO Tracker between August 27 and September 3, 2026, by injecting malicious code into "a.plerdy[.]com/public/js/click/main.js" Some of the compromised websites include a major industry trade association representing U.S. companies operating in the chemical industry, a far-right European political party, and a Bulgarian military-related website. It's suspected that the watering hole campaign may have been designed to target specific individuals rather than a broad effort. "It remains unclear whether the attackers intended to target visitors to specific websites or sought to compromise as many unpatched mobile devices as possible, indiscriminately exfiltrating data before selectively identifying and exploiting information of interest," Sekoia said. "However, several of these sites are likely to attract high-value or strategically important visitors in the context of the Russia-Ukraine war. This supply chain attack spread through high-value targets, such as army, special forces, and military equipment (ballistic, UAV) websites." Regardless of the method employed, all roads lead to the same payload: a JavaScript loader that profiles the visitor's device and web browser, and then serves appropriate next-stage malware. For iOS users, it leads to an exploit kit called DarkSword to harvest cookies and full device data. On Android, the malware is equipped to exfiltrate Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords without establishing persistence. No less than three different exploits have been identified - Class A, which targets iOS devices running iOS 16.7 and exploits CVE-2025-43529 (the same vulnerability exploited by DarkSword) and CVE-2024-27834 to deliver JavaScript malware for cookie theft. Class B, which targets iOS devices running iOS 18.5 and exploits the DarkSword exploit chain comprising CVE-2025-43529, CVE-2026-20700, CVE-2025-14174, CVE-2025-43510, and CVE-2025-43520 to deliver JavaScript malware for full device data exfiltration. This includes SMS messages and iMessages; Apple Mail Envelope Index and Protected Index SQLite databases; voicemail; WhatsApp and Telegram databases; iCloud Keychain, Wi-Fi passwords; contacts; call history; Safari browser history and cookies; photos; and data from Apple Health, Calendar, Notes, and iCloud Drive. Class C, which targets Android devices running Chrome versions from 139 through 145 (but explicitly excluding version 143 for reasons that remain presently unknown) and exploits CVE-2026-3910 and CVE-2025-27038 to achieve remote code execution, sandbox escape, privilege escalation, and ultimately deliver AndroSnitch to collect Chrome data and Wi-Fi passwords. In all three cases, the exfiltrated data is sent to the "ad.starx-net[.]com:8881/telemetry/v12" endpoint. The Android attack chain incorporates a check to determine whether the targeted device is a Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra by examining its model identifier (i.e., SM-S938B). If the device matches, the exploitation activity is terminated. AndroSnitch derives its name from its similarities to ANDROSNATCH, a Chrome cookie-stealing payload that Google documented in August 2024 in connection with a suspected APT29 watering hole campaign, which targeted Android users visiting a Mongolian government website by leveraging a Chrome exploit chain involving CVE-2024-5274 and CVE-2024-4671. "This operation also confirms the continued reuse of CSV [Commercial Surveillance Vendors] mobile exploit frameworks, such as DarkSword, by state-sponsored intrusion sets," Sekoia said. "The adoption of packaged N-day exploit chains lowers the cost and technical threshold required to conduct advanced mobile exploitation." Coruna and DarkSword Kits Evolve The development comes weeks after iVerify and Report URI detailed the P7 variant of DarkSword being delivered via half-click attacks that leverage ad-based infrastructure. In one case, the exploit is said to have been propagated through a malicious Instagram ad themed around the World Cup and served from "ad-track[.]live." The other pathway is part of a criminal campaign dubbed DeadTag, in which attackers acquire expired domains behind old analytics and advertising tags that are still loaded by thousands of websites. The idea is to serve malicious JavaScript to iPhone visitors and silently do the attacker's bidding. "It checks who's visiting," Report URI said. "Search engines, security scanners, automated browsers and anything else that looks like a bot gets nothing." The script then interacts with the attacker's server, which then decides the destination to which each visitor has to be redirected. The iPhone exploit paths that take advantage of DeadTag lead to the Coruna exploit kit for older iPhones running iOS version 13 to 17.2.1 and DarkSword P7 for iOS devices running 18.4 to 18.7. "These are not phishing pages or fake app downloads, both kits attack the browser itself," Report URI's Scott Helme said. "Simply opening the page is enough for your device to be compromised. There's nothing to tap, you don't need to click any link, nothing to install and no warning. If the iPhone is running a vulnerable version of iOS, the kit breaks out of the browser and installs spyware on the device." Other schemes lead to decoy Google redirects, betting and casino scam sign-up pages, search advertisements for car deals and dentists, and fake surveys and "you've won" prize pages. More than 660 expired and re-registered domains are part of the DeadTag network. According to an analysis published by Zimperium zLabs, campaigns distributing Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits have continued to evolve, with 608 domains delivering Coruna-family code as of October 2026. Although Coruna was initially developed by a nation-state actor for highly targeted operations, its subsequent leak following initial disclosure has made the toolkit widely accessible to multiple threat actors for their own campaigns. In many cases, the lure sites have been found to explicitly instruct visitors to exit their in-app browser or alternative iOS browser and open the link in Safari so as to trigger the exploit chain depending upon the device operating system. "Targets running iOS 17.2.1 or earlier receive the legacy Coruna framework (exhibiting byte-identical JavaScript payloads across multiple recovered configurations)," security researcher Santiago Rodriguez said. "Conversely, devices running later iOS builds receive a DarkSword-derived execution chain." "The analyzed distribution footprint spans dating portals, AI-companion platforms, cryptocurrency promotions, media streaming services, and – in several instances – compromised legitimate sites serving the kit via hidden iframes."

5yivqb.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security A critical flaw in Ruby on Rails could allow an unauthenticated attacker to write arbitrary files on an app's server by uploading a crafted file if the app processes uploads using ImageMagick. The Rails project disclosed the flaw in an advisory and fixed it in versions 8.1.4.1 and 8.0.5.2. The flaw is in Active Storage, the part of Rails that handles file uploads. Some apps store uploaded files using Active Storage's Disk service, which stores them on the server's disk. In those apps, an attacker could also read any file the app can read. Those files typically include the app's secret_key_base and its credentials for other systems, according to Rails.
