Reading them may in turn allow remote code execution or lateral movement into those systems. Rails rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. It is tracked as GHSA-f3w6-w445-fwh9 and does not yet have a CVE identifier. ImageMagick selects a format handler, which it calls a coder, based on the file's content. Some coders act on other files named inside the image, not on the image itself. Active Storage imposes no limits on which coders an upload can use, so the server's own ImageMagick policy was the only limit. The ImageMagick analyzer in Active Storage runs when a file is attached. Attaching the upload is enough to reach the flaw. The app does not have to make a variant (a transformed copy of the image) or a preview, or call analyze. An uploaded SVG file reached ImageMagick's MSL coder through that analyzer, according to the commit that fixed the flaw. MSL is a scripting coder that reads and writes files named by its script. Rails said one attack chain was reported to it, but it does "not assume it is the only one that exists." The advisory does not say whether the flaw has been exploited. The flaw was reported through HackerOne by RyotaK, a researcher at GMO Flatt Security. Which Rails Apps Are Affected An app is affected only if all three of these are true: It uses ImageMagick for Active Storage image processing. That is the setting config.active_storage.variant_processor = :mini_magick, the default for apps on load_defaults 6.1 or earlier. Its ImageMagick security policy does not already block the coders involved. Rails says the policies that Debian and Ubuntu ship do not. It accepts file uploads from untrusted users. To check the first condition, look at config.active_storage.variant_processor. If it is not set, the default depends on load_defaults: :mini_magick before 7.0, and :vips from 7.0 on. The same setting decides which library analyzes uploads, not only which one makes variants. Every Active Storage version before 8.0.5.2 is affected, as are 8.1 versions before 8.1.4.1. Release series older than 8.0 are no longer supported, and Rails will not release fixed versions for them. In July, Rails fixed a different critical Active Storage flaw, CVE-2026-66066, which affected apps that use libvips instead of ImageMagick. Apps using ImageMagick were not exposed to that flaw's attack path, but they can be exposed to this one. The same releases fix a second Active Storage flaw, GHSA-v924-7rp8-4mxh, which Rails rates high with a CVSS score of 8.8. Active Storage passed uploads to ImageMagick and FFmpeg under temporary file names that kept the uploaded file's extension. Those tools can pick a decoder from the extension when a file's content does not show its format. So an attacker who chose an upload's filename and declared its content type could choose the decoder that processes it. What to Do Rails strongly recommends upgrading as soon as possible. The two releases fix 21 security issues in total. The fixed versions ship an ImageMagick security policy. MiniMagick is the Ruby gem Active Storage uses to call ImageMagick. In its default setup, every ImageMagick command it runs applies the policy, not only commands from Active Storage. The policy blocks the MSL coder; coders that read or delete files other than the image; coders that fetch remote or local references or display them on a screen; every coder backed by Ghostscript, along with the gs delegate; and @filename indirection. Upgrade to Rails 8.1.4.1 or 8.0.5.2. Apps on :mini_magick also need mini_magick 5.1 or later, or they raise an error at boot. Rails 8.0 gets security fixes only until November 7, 2026, under its maintenance policy. Confirm that the app loads the new policy, as the Active Storage guide describes, by running bin/rails runner 'puts MiniMagick.identify { |i| i.list "policy" }'. Check whether the shipped policy reaches the app at all. It does not reach an app that replaces MiniMagick.cli_env after boot, clears the environment with MiniMagick.cli_prefix, or installs its own MiniMagick::Shell. Such an app must put the rules in ImageMagick's system policy. Apps that use GraphicsMagick get no protection from the shipped policy, because GraphicsMagick does not read ImageMagick policies. Check the server's own ImageMagick policy. The shipped policy adds to it rather than replacing it. A rule there that allows a coder, including a wildcard such as pattern="*", overrides the shipped policy's block on that coder. If the app renders PDF or PostScript files through ImageMagick, re-allow the gs delegate and the coders it uses in the server's policy.xml. If you cannot upgrade yet, copy the rules of the shipped policy, activestorage/lib/active_storage/image_magick/policy.xml, into ImageMagick's system policy, such as /etc/ImageMagick-7/policy.xml. At a minimum, block the MSL coder, the Ghostscript coders, and the gs delegate. Rails also published the fix as patches for 8.1 and 8.0. Apps on release series older than 8.0 can use that workaround or upgrade to 8.0 or later. Rails' workarounds for the second flaw only change how FFmpeg is used. None of them covers ImageMagick. If the app stores attachments with the Disk service, change secret_key_base and every other secret the app process can read. That includes the master key, everything config/credentials.yml.enc holds, storage and database credentials, and third-party tokens. Do not keep an exposed secret as a fallback. The advisory does not explain how to check whether an app has already been targeted.

lovedy.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Cloud Security Two flaws in the Xen hypervisor allow a malicious guest virtual machine (VM) to read and write the memory of other VMs on the same host, including dom0. Dom0 is the VM that, by default, has full permissions and manages the others. Patches are out, and there is no known mitigation, the Xen Project said in an advisory on November 3. All Xen versions from 4.6 onward are vulnerable, while 4.5 and earlier are not. The flaws are tracked as CVE-2026-102703 and CVE-2026-102704, under Xen advisory XSA-523. The Xen Project credited AI company Anthropic with finding the flaws using its Claude model. Stephan Lipp of Ada Logics then validated the finding, and the CodeAnt AI Security Research Team later independently reported the same issue. The flaws are in grant copy, the operation Xen uses to copy data between VMs. Each VM tells Xen which of its memory pages other VMs may use, and Xen checks those permissions. To save time on a batch of copies within the same memory page, Xen reuses checks it has already made. In some cases, it did not check again when it should have. That mistake is what lets a malicious guest read and write memory it does not own. XCP-ng, an open-source virtualization platform built around Xen, said in its update notes that "a single compromised guest can break out of its isolation and take over the whole host." Xen's advisory does not mention any attacks that exploit the flaws or specify what access within the VM an attacker needs. Qubes OS is a security-focused desktop operating system that keeps software in separate Xen-based compartments called qubes. A bulletin said that every supported release and configuration is affected. Its fix is for Qubes 4.3, the only release it still supports. Because every Xen version from 4.6 on is vulnerable, other products built on those versions are affected until their makers add the XSA-523 patches. As of November 4, Debian's security tracker listed the xen package in its bookworm, trixie, and forky releases as vulnerable, and in sid as fixed. Fixes and Restarts by Platform These are the fixes published so far: Xen source: the advisory has patches for xen-unstable to Xen 4.19.x, and for Xen 4.18.x to 4.17.x. Xen 4.6 to 4.16: the advisory has no patch for these versions. Xen 4.16's security support ended on December 2, 2024. XCP-ng 8.3: xen-4.17.7-4.2.xcpng8.3, released November 3. Hosts must be rebooted. Vates, which backs XCP-ng, rates the impact as Critical. Qubes OS 4.3: Xen packages 4.19.6-3 in dom0. Dom0 must be restarted, and Anti Evil Maid users must reseal their secret passphrase because the new Xen binaries change PCR18 and PCR19. Qubes told users on November 3 to keep installing updates as normal. The fixed packages were then in its security-testing repository, due to move to the stable one over the next two weeks after community testing. XSA-523 is separate from XSA-500, an earlier grant copy flaw that Xen disclosed on July 28, and it has its own patches.

3xx1rk.text: Nearly every agent security pitch now ends on the same promise: the product stops the bad action in real time. The promise holds for one kind of agent, the kind whose traffic passes through a gateway the enterprise owns. Most agents never touch one. One recent case shows what that gap looks like in practice. An employee asked an AI assistant to trigger a mass-email automation. The automation hit a recipient-limit policy and failed, so the assistant, which was also connected to the employee's personal mailbox, offered to send the batch from there instead. The employee approved without registering that the assistant was about to route around the sanctioned system. An unknown number of external recipients received email from a personal account rather than the approved channel. No jailbreak was involved. The assistant did exactly what it was built to do, and the fix was not retraining a model. It was a single runtime rule that blocks any attempt to reach more than fifty external domains and explains to the user what the tool is about to do. Knowing where to apply a rule like that depends on seeing which agents exist, what they are connected to and what normal looks like for each. That visibility is the part most runtime pitches skip. The runtime is the application, not the pipe The year's largest agent launches placed agents inside platforms the buyer does not own. Claudeforce runs Claude inside Salesforce's trust boundary, Claude Tag lives inside Slack and Copilot lives inside Microsoft 365. Workday, which says AI now drives more than a quarter of its new annual contract value, runs its agents inside Workday. In each case the agent's tools are the application's features, its knowledge is the application's data and its permissions are the application's permission model. A gateway can only inspect what passes through it. An agent that runs inside Salesforce, fires from a Flow, reads CRM records and writes case comments sends nothing past an inspection point, and the same is true of a Copilot agent assembling a document from SharePoint or a Slack-native agent reading years of channel history. The OWASP Agentic Skills Top 10 describes this gap as the "unreachable skill" scenario under AST09, No Governance: a capability deployed inside a third-party platform where no external scanner can go. Security has made a move like this before. Firewalls once inspected packets by source, destination and port, until applications stopped mapping cleanly to ports and malicious traffic began to look identical to legitimate traffic. The inspection point moved up the stack to the application, where the signal lives. Agent runtime needs the same move, with a complication the earlier one never faced: the application layer belongs to someone else. A gateway-only strategy protects the agents an enterprise hosts itself, which are the fewest and the slowest growing. The inspection point is also a target In March 2026, attackers compromised LiteLLM, the open-source gateway that routes agent traffic to model providers. The malicious packages were live for about forty minutes, and CloudSEK later put the exposure at more than 2,500 organizations. LiteLLM is the kind of component a security-conscious team adds on purpose to watch AI traffic, which made the inspection point itself the attack vector. None of this argues against gateways. It argues against treating any single component as the whole strategy. A gateway is more software in the supply chain, with its own release pipeline and dependencies, and it concentrates exactly the traffic an attacker wants. When enforcement is a shared component, its failure is a shared failure. A millisecond verdict needs a memory Runtime decisions are made in milliseconds, and the hard cases are the gray ones. A support agent pulling customer data may be doing its job or exfiltrating it. A coding agent reading a repository may be gathering context or performing reconnaissance. A finance agent creating an OAuth connection may be doing integration work or making the first move of a compromise. The action alone does not carry the verdict. The agent's identity and owner, its permissions, its normal behavior, the sensitivity of the data, the destination and the delegation chain behind the request do. Chains raise the bar. Enforcement that evaluates only the last hop sees an authorized agent performing an action it has permission for, and misses that the authority arrived through a chain nobody approved. Judging the whole chain at runtime means already knowing it, and that knowledge cannot be assembled in a millisecond. Enforcement without that map is an air-traffic controller with a radio but no radar: commands can be issued, but the picture of which plane is headed where does not exist. What real agent runtime looks like Three properties follow. Enforcement has to sit where the agents are, across several vantage points such as native platform hooks, API-level controls, the MCP layer, the browser and the endpoint, rather than at a single gateway. Every verdict has to be computed against a live map of identity, permissions, connectivity and activity (IPCA), plus data sensitivity and delegation, which is what turns the gray cases into judgments. And the response menu has to be wider than block. Mature enforcement is graduated. It allows the known-good, warns where justification is plausible, redacts where the data is the problem and blocks where the chain is hostile. It routes the highest-stakes actions to a human and keeps a kill switch for the provably compromised agent that suspends it, revokes its grants and preserves the trail. Every verdict is logged with its full causal path, because an incident review and a regulator want the same five things: the agent, the chain, the data, the destination and the policy. Do not buy the end state Irregular's Dan Lahav calls the mistake the end-state fallacy: assuming the properties of the eventual equilibrium apply to the transition actually underway. In runtime purchasing, it is the belief that inline enforcement will eventually see everything, so the unglamorous layers can be skipped. That end state is not available this year from any vendor at any price. Runtime coverage is partial and platform hooks are arriving unevenly. What can be bought now, everywhere, is the stack runtime depends on: discovery across every vantage point, posture on every platform, identity and ownership for every agent and context for every decision. Each enforcement point that opens later then snaps into a map that already knows what normal looks like. The full argument for where enforcement belongs is in From AI Runtime to Agent Runtime. The first ninety days, in order A sequence that follows the stack bottom-up looks like this. Window The work How to know it is real Weeks 1 to 2: get the number Connect what is already running (the identity provider, major platforms, network tools, the email layer) and let discovery work across every vantage point at once. No gateway deployment, no endpoint rollout, no rerouted traffic. Time to first insight is days, not quarters. The discovered population is several multiples of the list IT keeps. Weeks 3 to 6: names and configurations Every discovered agent gets a named human owner or is suspended. Configuration debt is triaged, starting with the platforms hosting the most reachable agents: guest-user exposures, intake features wired to agent triggers, sharing rules from three years ago. Guardrails go on customer-facing and privileged agents first. A human raises a hand within a day when asked "whose is this?" Weeks 7 to 12: the queue and the path Context-aware risk tiering so review starts with the agent that can actually hurt the business, a least-privilege review cadence on the top tier and a sanctioned route for business teams to ship agents with secure defaults. Any critical rating can be explained as a chain, and builders are offered a path instead of only a block. The enablement path matters because the builders are coming either way. Blocking teaches evasion, while a good path teaches compliance. Teams can place themselves with a four-level test. Blind means the board's three questions (how many agents exist, what they can reach and who is accountable) have no current answer. Inventoried means the population is discovered, counted and refreshed continuously. Governed means every agent has an owner, posture is managed against baselines and risk is tiered with context. Instrumented means enforcement operates where agents run, with graduated verdicts and a full causal path in every alert. Most enterprises are at the first level, whatever the policy document says, and a vendor selling instrumentation to a blind organization is selling enforcement that can act but cannot judge. Seven questions that sort vendors Every vendor deck now says agent security. These questions separate vendors that built for the problem from vendors that renamed a product, because each is easy to answer well only if the architecture underneath exists. Ask What a good answer looks like Can you find agents that never authenticate through SSO? Yes, across several independent vantage points, each seeing something the others cannot. For an agent you rated critical, show me the chain. A complete, reachable attack path (capability, reachability, asset) that an analyst can verify, not an aggregate score. Does the same finding produce different severities on different agents? Yes, demonstrated on a sandboxed agent and a customer-facing one. When one agent invokes another, can you reconstruct the delegation chain? Original requester, every hop and the final action. An audit trail that starts at the last agent is not one. What context feeds an allow, block or redact verdict? Identity, permissions, delegation and data sensitivity, not the prompt alone. What happens to my protection if your enforcement component is compromised? A specific answer that addresses the LiteLLM incident directly. How long until I see my real agent inventory? Days. A quarter is a different product. Platforms built around the map rather than the individual agent can answer these directly. One leading example is Reco, whose Reco Graph connects every human and non-human identity, application, permission and agent action into a single live view, so that reach, not configuration, is the unit of analysis. One measured program that applied this approach moved its posture score from 47% to 91% across 21 platforms in 30 days. Learn more about Reco's agent discovery at reco.ai/platform. The full ninety-day sequence, the four-level self-assessment and all fifteen vendor questions are in The Agent Security Checklist: Your First 90 Days. About Reco Reco is the leader in Agent Security. The Reco Platform secures agents and their operating environments where applications, identities, permissions, and workflows intersect. It discovers an organization's entire third-party ecosystem, prioritizes real risk over alert volume and remediates with precision across every human identity, agent, app and permission in the environment. Built on the Reco Graph, with new integrations delivered in hours through the Reco Factory and pre-built agent and app intelligence from the Reco Library. Security leaders at Fortune 500 enterprises choose Reco to bring order to agent proliferation and the chain reactions that follow. With more than 280 app integrations, more than 1,000 detection controls and more than 1 million agents detected, Reco brings agent security, posture management and threat detection together in one place. Learn more at reco.ai. See what is running in your environment. Agent360 is a free assessment that shows which agents and apps are active, what they can reach and who owns them. It runs on a read-only API with no software to install and returns a written security summary and a prioritized remediation plan in five business days. Request a free Agent360 assessment.

h8fp9k.text: A China-aligned threat actor known as SlippyNunchucks has been attributed to a Domain Name System (DNS) hijacking operation abusing insecure HTTP communications in Windows versions of Sogou Input Method as part of a surveillance campaign designed to deploy an implant called DarkVigil (aka FDMTP). The campaign, observed starting July 1, 2026, is assessed to have targeted organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals in Hong Kong, Thailand, Japan, Vietnam, Oman, and Sri Lanka, according to ESET. "DarkVigil implants are typically deployed through popular Chinese applications," ESET researcher Anh Ho said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "By abusing these applications, the SlippyNunchucks threat actor has been able to reach Chinese-speaking users across Asia and Europe." Some of the applications abused by the adversary include Sogou Input Method, QuickFox, QingTalk, MiYunChat, SoftCam, and tawk.to. Active since at least September 15, 2023, SlippyNunchucks is known for targeting organizations and Chinese-speaking individuals across South and East Asia. These attacks led to the deployment of a modular .NET framework that includes DarkVigil and a set of over 20 plugins. Although the use of the backdoor has been previously linked to Mustang Panda, ESET said it found no tactical overlaps between the threat actor and DarkVigil-related activity in its telemetry, prompting it to classify it as a distinct intrusion set. Earlier this August, Fortinet's FortiGuard Incident Response Team detailed the threat actor's supply chain compromise of the QuickFox VPN and network acceleration tool to deliver DarkVigil. According to the Slovakian cybersecurity company, the adversary shifted to exploiting Sogou Input Method, a popular Chinese-language input method editor developed by Tencent, as a delivery vector three days after QuickFox released a clean version of its program. Specifically, the attack involves hijacking the app's branded vocabulary promotion mechanism to serve a malicious configuration, which ultimately paves the way for the deployment of the malware via SGTool.exe, a legitimate Sogou Input Method component that functions as a multi-purpose task dispatcher. In a clean environment, the executable sends an HTTP request to the "config.pinyin.sogou[.]com/api/brandScd/getBrandScd.php" endpoint to fetch a configuration. But in the attack discovered by ESET, the DNS resolution of the domain is tampered with to resolve it to one of the two staging servers - 47.239.250[.]102 (sogou-cdn[.]com) 47.237.122[.]175 (dev.soft-png-cdn.com) The consequence of this DNS hijacking was that HTTP requests to the "getBrandScd.php" endpoint were routed to one of the staging servers, which then responded with a malicious configuration. The configuration, for its part, instructs the binary to download two additional payloads from "sogou-cdn[.]com" and launch the malware via DLL sideloading - A legitimate Adobe executable ("biz_helper.exe") A rogue DLL ("libcef.dll") containing DarkVigil DarkVigil is notable for its use of Duplex Message Transport Protocol (DMTP) for command-and-control (C2), allowing the client to execute and orchestrate plugins received from an attacker-controlled server to facilitate persistence or data collection. Following responsible disclosure, Tencent addressed the vulnerability (CVE-2026-120422) in version 16.10, released on October 29, 2026, by migrating the affected HTTP requests to HTTPS. SlippyNunchucks is suspected to operate keeping the interests of the Chinese government in mind, with ESET describing it as a nation-state surveillance effort. "Although SlippyNunchucks targets organizations and individuals across multiple sectors, we discovered significant surveillance activity against an organization operating Chinese-language online betting platforms in Sri Lanka, Hong Kong, and the Philippines," ESET said. "The targeting of this organization is notable given China's restrictions on gambling, including criminal penalties for operating gambling businesses and organizing Chinese citizens to gamble abroad." This is not the first time China-nexus threat actors have weaponized the Sogou Input Method as an entry point for malware distribution. In September 2026, Gen Digital said a now-patched vulnerability in the input method editor (CVE-2026-51990) was exploited by UNC3569 to deliver a backdoor dubbed GRAYRABBIT by means of a crafted link. "The vulnerability chains three separate weaknesses into a single, one-click exploit: unvalidated command-line argument injection in the sgbiz: custom protocol handler, unrestricted URL navigation in a CEF-based WebView, and a severely outdated, unsandboxed Chromium browser engine [susceptible to CVE-2021-38003]," Gen Digital said.

uh5mge.text: Russian authorities have arrested three suspected members of a threat group known as VasyGrek and dismantled its criminal infrastructure. Also known as Fluffy Wolf, the threat actor has a history of targeting Russian and international companies since 2016. The Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Russian Federation (MVD) said members of the group are "suspected of embezzling funds from the accounts of organizations, as well as creating, distributing, and using malicious software." In one September 2025 case highlighted by the ministry, the attackers are said to have sent a phishing email to an unnamed organization, masquerading it as business correspondence and instructing recipients to open a reconciliation report that triggered the execution of malware. The incident resulted in losses of 660,000 rubles ($8,000) from the organization's bank account, with the attackers transferring the funds to accounts under their control. "The attacks utilized a vast network of phishing domains imitating financial and accounting service websites, as well as virtual servers located in foreign countries," MVD said. "Tools for covert remote administration were acquired from the dark web." The rare law enforcement action saw Russian authorities conducting searches at the suspects' residences and the office premises they used to conduct the operations. It also led to the seizure of computer equipment, communication devices, and other items of evidentiary value. According to reports from Russian cybersecurity company BI.ZONE and F6, VasyGrek is assessed to be a financially motivated threat actor that gains initial access by sending phishing emails with attachments disguised as financial documents. Some of the key tools in its arsenal include off-the-shelf stealers and trojans, like MetaStealer, PureCrypter, PureLogs Stealer, WarZone RAT, XMRig, BurnsRAT, PureHVNC, PureRAT, Pay2Key, and PowerLoader, as well as legitimate remote access software such as Remote Utilities. In a report published this week, Kaspersky said it recorded over 100 attempted attacks orchestrated by VasyGrek against organizations in Russia, Belarus, and Kazakhstan between January and September 2026. These attacks have also been observed using decoy documents to drop a Golang backdoor capable of executing arbitrary commands on the infected device. The attacks primarily singled out entities in the metallurgical sector, along with wholesale suppliers of raw materials and industrial supplies and government agencies. Other targets included organizations in the healthcare, oil and gas, energy, finance, and agriculture sectors. "The group expanded its attack geography: while previously its primary target was Russian organizations, this year, potential victims also included companies from Belarus and Kazakhstan," Nikita Nazarov, head of advanced threat research at Kaspersky, said. "The attackers used multi-stage infection schemes and legitimate online services to host malicious components, which helped conceal their activity and hinder attack analysis." The development comes as BI.ZONE it detected multiple attacks targeting Russian organizations using malware families like LxBase RAT, CoreRAT, and NightStrike RAT. While LxBase RAT, a commercial trojan that costs $119 per month, is distributed via mass phishing campaigns, CoreRAT infection chains make use of phishing emails containing 7zSFX and Rust droppers for delivery. The activity has been attributed to Core Werewolf, which is assessed to share some level of overlap with Vortex Werewolf. Attacks deploying NightStrike RAT have been associated with a hacktivist-turned-cyber espionage cluster dubbed Insolent Werewolf. Initial access is achieved using ClickFix-style attacks to deploy NetSupport Manager to gain remote access. "Insolent Werewolf also utilizes Octowave Loader to deploy AdaptixC2 and Havoc post‑exploitation framework implants in compromised systems," BI.ZONE said, adding the group's malware arsenal includes other remote access trojans like CapDoor and NightWire. "A RAT written in C++, NightStrike has presumably been created by the developer of NightWire, based on similarities in coding style. Utilizing diverse frameworks and their own custom malware allows the adversary to tailor tooling to specific attack conditions and reduce the likelihood of detection."

1q4f2us.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Mobile Security A critical Android flaw could allow an attacker to run code on a phone without any user action remotely, Google said in its November security bulletin. The flaw, CVE-2026-58868, affects Android 14 through 17. Phones get the fix with security patch level 2026-11-01 or later, which phone makers and carriers send on their own schedules. As of November 4, Google's bulletin did not report any attacks exploiting its flaws. None of them was in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog, kept by the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, as of its November 3 update. The flaw is a possible out-of-bounds write caused by a heap buffer overflow in the onOutputReceived function of the file FrameDecoder.cpp. Neither the bulletin nor the flaw's CVE record says how an attacker would reach that code. Google's Critical rating assumes that the protections built into Android and Google's services are turned off or bypassed. Older versions, such as Android 12 and 13, are not listed as affected by the flaw. Google's records do not say whether they contain it. How to Check Your Phone Google's help page gives these steps: Open the Settings app. Tap About phone, or About tablet, then Android version. Find the dates for the Android security update and the Google Play system update. The Android security update date is the phone's security patch level. A date of 2026-11-01 or later covers CVE-2026-58868 and the other flaws in the Framework, System, and Android runtime components. A date of 2026-11-05 or later covers every flaw in the November bulletin, including those in the kernel and in parts from Arm, Imagination Technologies, MediaTek, Unisoc and Qualcomm. Google sets two dates so phone makers can ship a set of fixes common to all Android devices sooner. It encourages them to include every fix in the bulletin. Phones running Android 10 or later may also receive some fixes through Google Play system updates. This month's list for those updates includes another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58876. CVE-2026-58868 is not on that list, so the date to check for it is the Android security update. The bulletin gives no workaround for phones that cannot install the update yet. A Remote Denial-of-Service Flaw in Android's Text-Message Code Another Critical flaw, CVE-2026-58882, could allow a remote denial-of-service attack with no user interaction, according to its CVE record. It is in decodeWapPdu, a function in Android's code for WAP Push messages that arrive via SMS. On October 29, a researcher who publishes as Mark B posted a write-up called "SMS of Death" about a bug in the same function. Neither the bulletin nor the CVE record says whether CVE-2026-58882 is that bug. One malformed WAP Push message crashes com.android.phone and ends any active call, including emergency calls, according to the write-up. In tests on several phone models, the crash happened every time. The attacker needs only the target's phone number, and the message never shows up in the inbox. The phone retries the message each time it starts, so it can crash on startup until the message is removed. A proof-of-concept app that sends such a message from one phone to another is public. Phones running Android 12 and 13 run the same code but do not receive the fix that newer versions do, the researcher says. Other Critical Flaws Google's November bulletin lists 216 vulnerabilities, 23 of them rated Critical. Two more Critical flaws could allow remote code execution: CVE-2026-58876 and CVE-2026-58936, both in Android's System component. Six Critical flaws are in the kernel, two of them in Bluetooth code. The most severe kernel flaw could allow a remote attacker to gain elevated privileges without user interaction. The 2026-11-05 patch level also fixes Critical flaws in MediaTek modem code and in a closed-source Qualcomm component. In its November bulletin, MediaTek describes its Critical modem flaws as out-of-bounds writes and says it is not aware of any active exploitation.

k8eu29.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 04, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added a security flaw in WordPress Core to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing evidence of active exploitation. The high-severity vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-119977 (CVSS score: 8.1), is a case of Time-of-check Time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition that could be exploited to achieve arbitrary code execution on affected servers. Patches for the flaw were released late last month. "WordPress Core contains a time-of-check time-of-use (TOCTOU) race condition vulnerability that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on the server during the upgrade window," CISA said. "This is due to predictable, web-accessible staging paths used during full-package core upgrades." Details of the flaw emerged last week when Wordfence said exploiting the vulnerability does not require an account on the site. That said, it does require an attacker to exploit a brief window during a complete Core update that could allow unauthenticated code execution. During the first 21 hours after public disclosure, the WordPress security company said it recorded more than 18,500 requests targeting staged "setup-config.php" installer paths. As of writing, 12,632 attacks attempting to exploit the flaw have been blocked in the last 24 hours. Telemetry data from Previdian shows that three exploitation attempts have been recorded against its honeypot censors from an IP address geolocated in the U.K. The exploitation events were observed on October 30, 2026. With exploitation now officially confirmed by CISA, Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies have time until November 6, 2026, to apply the fixes.

boozc6.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 03, 2026Password Security / Incident Response Customers of the mSecure password manager are being urged to act now to protect the confidential information they store in it, possibly by changing passwords, resetting two-factor authentication (2FA), and removing passkeys. The warning came in an email sent on November 3 in the name of developer mSeven Software. It says the company recently learned of suspicious activity linked to the app but does not say what happened or whether anyone's stored data was exposed. The email says it went to current and former mSecure customers. A customer who received it posted its text in a thread on mSecure's support forum on November 3. As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, mSeven had posted nothing about the email on mSecure's X and Facebook accounts. No staff member had replied in that forum thread. The email says mSeven started an investigation, took steps to limit the problem and brought in outside cybersecurity experts. It does not name the systems involved, say when the activity happened or whether it has stopped, or give the number of people who received the email. mSecure can sync a customer's vault through mSecure Cloud, Dropbox, iCloud or Wi-Fi. The email does not say whether it matters which of these a customer uses. mSecure 7 can keep passkeys and 2FA codes in the vault next to passwords, on its Essentials plan and above. The email's advice is about protecting information stored in mSecure. The email does not say whether the 2FA and passkey steps cover those stored items, the mSecure account's own sign-in, or both. mSecure says vault data is encrypted on the customer's device before it is synced, and that even its developers cannot access customers' information. In mSecure 6.1.5 for Android, mSeven could, in theory, access stored data, according to Germany's Federal Office for Information Security (BSI), which found this in a study published in December 2025. The BSI tested only that version, and its results may have changed with later updates. The email does not say whether the suspicious activity reached vault data or the keys that protect it. What the Email Asks Customers to Do The email offers its steps as possibilities and does not say which accounts to deal with first or how to carry out each step. It also does not say whether customers should keep using mSecure, including to store their new passwords. As of 18:00 UTC on November 3, the newest iPhone version of mSecure in Apple's App Store was 7.1.0, released on October 23.

v3v437.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 03, 2026Data Breach / Cyber Attack Blockchain infrastructure provider Chainstack on Tuesday disclosed that it was targeted in a cyber attack that allowed an unauthorized party to gain access to some parts of its infrastructure. The incident is assessed to be part of a large-scale, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered attack campaign that came to light last week. "An external attacker gained unauthorized access to part of Chainstack's infrastructure through a third-party component," the company said. "We detected the intrusion, cut the access paths, and are hardening our systems." According to the timeline of events shared by Chainstack, the attacker gained access to a development environment on October 26, 2026, and then escalated their access to break into "some parts of our production environment." The intrusion was subsequently detected on October 31, 2026, and the attacker's access was cut off that same day, the company noted. As part of the digital break-in, the threat actor is said to have accessed a database containing customer account information, including organization names, account holder names, the email addresses of organization’s members on Chainstack, and password hashes. "The attacker also had access to systems holding node credentials," Chainstack said. "We have no evidence they were read, but we are treating them as exposed and ask customers to rotate them." Besides rotating the node credentials, customers are advised to regenerate their platform API keys, update passwords -- including other services where the same password has been reused -- and remain alert to potential phishing attempts. Although Chainstack did not disclose any specifics about the attack, it's assessed to share overlaps with a campaign undertaken by a China-linked cluster to target high-value firms using ARTEX. WorkOS Targeted by ARTEX Too The development comes as API platform WorkOS also disclosed a security incident that involved the same autonomous AI agent framework to conduct offensive security operations. The incident, which was discovered on October 30, 2026, was limited to its GTM systems, and did not affect production systems or customer platform data. The accessed data includes - Business contact details (Names, email addresses, phone numbers, job titles, and company affiliations stored in its customer relationship management system) Business account and relationship information (Customer account histories and information about sales and customer-relationship information) Customer communications (Summaries and excerpts from sales calls, support discussions, and customer Slack conversations) Operational metadata (Information about customers' use of WorkOS products, including product usage and connection or directory health) The breach is part of a growing trend in which AI agents are being employed to devise tailored attack strategies and automate different phases of the intrusion. "This increases the speed and scale of attacks that exploit weaknesses such as exposed applications and stolen credentials," WorkOS said. "It increases the need for timely remediation and monitoring that can connect suspicious activity across systems." Last week, blockchain analysis firm Chainalysis also revealed that it detected an "external actor using offensive agentic techniques" to obtain access to its systems and internal tools. As of November 2, 2026, the company has proactively taken its Reactor and Data Solutions products offline. "We are closely monitoring these systems for unusual activity and will keep you apprised of new information so you can make informed decisions for your business and operations," Chainalysis said. Another organization to be hit by ARTEX is the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). The September 21, 2026, breach involved the exploitation of two zero-day flaws in the open-source Zammad ticketing system (CVE-2026-102489 and CVE-2026-102490), enabling attackers to escalate privileges, run code remotely, and exfiltrate data.

1y8zigo.text: Binance on Tuesday said the record-setting theft of $6.43 billion in assets from the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange was the culmination of a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" that involved the use of a tampered Homebrew installation and recruitment-themed social engineering attack targeting two of its engineers. "It was not a single isolated breach or a simple phishing incident," the company said. "The attackers combined a range of techniques, including social engineering by fake recruitment interviews, malicious software downloads, compromised internal AI tooling, endpoint compromise, and an advanced transaction-authorisation method." The starting point has been traced back to a supply chain attack targeting one of its engineers from the Wallet DevOps team (named "Engineer A"), who downloaded a trojanized Homebrew installer to install a popular artificial intelligence (AI) tool after searching for it on a search engine. The incident occurred in June 2026. Although Binance said it detected the attack and rotated all related credentials as a precautionary step, the company said information about "Engineer A's role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker." The second part of the attack occurred in September 2026, with the threat actor contacting another engineer (named "Engineer B") via a legitimate job-hunting platform by disguising themselves as a Project Director. The Project Director persona arranged a first-round interview with a human resources (HR) representative, which was then followed by a second-round interview with an individual claiming to be the CEO of a non-existent company. Binance did not disclose details of the fake company. Over the course of the first-round video interview, the HR representative shared a social media account, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in an attempt to build credibility and establish trust. The second round, on the other hand, took place on a popular social chat app. "Near the end of the interview, Engineer B was instructed to download an 'assignment' containing a malicious code repository onto his work computer," Binance said. "The repository contained malicious code that executed during the setup process, initiating a series of unauthorized activities." The undetected malware utilized advanced obfuscation and evasion techniques, including substituting a legitimate development tool component with a poisoned version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server. In addition, the threat actor took steps to cover up tracks by removing forensic artifacts related to the compromise. The intrusion moved to the next stage on October 20, 2026, when the adversary leveraged Engineer B's compromised computer and abused an internal AI tool to gain control over Engineer A and another Wallet Software Engineer C. "The attacker soon discovered Wallet DevOps Engineer A had a container deployment permission token on his computer," Binance explained. "On 29 October between 17:15 and 19:56, the attacker logged onto Software Engineer C's computer, used the credentials stolen from Wallet DevOps Engineer A, deployed a container, and triggered a malicious script to launch the attack." The attack ultimately exploited its unauthorized access to an internal wallet signing service to initiate transactions outside the normal withdrawal process. In response to the incident, Binance has reconstructed the affected wallet system in a new environment, as well as rebuilt the internal AI tool and access controls. Other steps taken as of November 3 are listed below - Replaced affected devices. Decommissioned credentials and tokens related to affected engineers. Completed enhanced security scans across all employee devices. Enhanced AI-based behavioural anomaly detection. Strengthened wallet-service risk controls. Worked with law enforcement, blockchain intelligence firms, and industry partners to trace and freeze affected assets. "The entry points identified as having been used in the attack have been closed. Systems touched in the attack path have been rebuilt or replaced," Binance said. "We have also implemented tighter device controls, enhanced wallet-service risk controls and expanded AI-based behavioural anomaly detection." "We are increasing investment in AI-enabled detection, endpoint protection, developer-environment security and behavioural anomaly monitoring." Since the start of the year, Binance is estimated to have foiled 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, underscoring the persistent nature of the attacks targeting the cryptocurrency industry. "The techniques include fraudulent job interviews, malicious software disguised as popular developer tools, compromised software packages and browser extensions, fake video conferencing applications, and social engineering campaigns designed to steal credentials or deploy remote access malware," Binance said.

uxmlpx.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 03, 2026Vulnerability / Network Security Barracuda has disclosed details of two vulnerabilities affecting its products that, if chained together, could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and gain root access to a susceptible device. The vulnerabilities, a pre-authentication authorization bypass vulnerability and a command injection vulnerability, have been assigned the CVE identifiers CVE-2026-116606 (CVSS score: 9.3) and CVE-2026-111560 (CVSS score: 8.6), respectively. While CVE-2026-116606 only affects Email Security Gateway, CVE-2026-111560 impacts the following Barracuda products - Email Security Gateway Load Balancer Application Delivery Controller Message Archiver WAF Control Center Web Application Firewall Web Security Gateway "Successful exploitation requires an attacker to have access to the administrative interface of an affected product," Barracuda said. "If exploited in combination, these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to bypass authorization controls and obtain root access to the device." Barracuda said that organizations that do not expose their administrative interfaces to the internet are less vulnerable to the attack path, urging customers to follow the steps below - Restrict access to administrative interfaces to trusted internal networksUse appropriate network access controls to limit exposure "Customers using these products should verify that their systems are running the latest firmware versions and have received all security patches," it added. "If firmware on a device is multiple versions out of date, customers may need to perform more than one update."

1amhdkw.text: Google on Monday warned that threat actors are hijacking enterprise access to Large Language Models (LLMs) to fraudulently leverage expensive computing resources and AI services. The tactic is called LLMjacking, a form of resource hijacking adapted for the LLM era, where an attacker obtains an API key through phishing, source code leaks, misconfigured environments, or exposed client-side code to gain unauthorized access to an organization's LLM accounts, while the legitimate owner covers the consumption costs. Such attacks have a wide geographical footprint, with impacted entities located in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific across the financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors. "Unlike the gradual resource consumption associated with cryptojacking, LLMJacking can generate large spikes in fraudulent cloud charges in a matter of hours," Google Threat Intelligence Group and Mandiant said in a report shared with The Hacker News. "Across individual incidents, we observed fraudulent charges associated with resource consumption exceeding $100,000 USD in a single day, with cumulative charges at some organizations reaching $1 million USD before access was revoked." On one end of the spectrum are low-level resource theft that involves the manipulation of customer support chatbots to conduct unauthorized tasks like code generation. LLMjacking is on the other end, as they target the backend model resources directly by identifying publicly exposed LLM endpoints or obtaining valid LLM API keys. The most common initial access vector has been exposed or stolen cloud identity tokens, including IAM credentials, Service Account keys, GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs), and active session tokens, which allow an attacker to establish an initial foothold into target organizations' infrastructure. This includes a threat actor called UNC6993, which is said to have breached a cloud instance through a misconfigured Service Account key and used it to obtain access to an LLM API. "UNC6993 also hosted a session hijacking page masquerading as an application portal to join a group of LLM users," Google said. "This page tricks users into navigating to the legitimate LLM service website, and pasting their raw JSON payload containing an active access token, which was then posted to the backend API to bypass password and multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls." In another case, an unknown attacker has been observed leveraging a stolen Personal Access Token to access private code repositories, following it up with the exploitation of a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running within a containerized cloud environment. Other initial access routes include the compromise of IAM credentials of corporate users to programmatically generate fresh access keys to bypass MFA safeguards, as well as the use of a hacked cloud Service Account key with broad project permissions and LLM API keys obtained from public GitHub repositories. Upon successfully gaining a foothold, the threat actors waste no time escalating privileges, burrowing deeper into the network, establishing persistence, and conducting internal reconnaissance to identify targets and further cloud credentials for lateral movement. Some of the observed tactics are listed below - Enumerate cloud services, code repositories, and data stores for sensitive credentials. Perform internal reconnaissance across multiple cloud regions to map available services and identity policies. Clone sensitive codebases to search for hard-coded secrets, configuration variables, and developer credentials. Scan access logs to identify credentials for secondary cloud environments. Run targeted database queries to harvest additional credentials. Abuse cloud identity permissions and virtual machine configurations to escalate privileges and maintain persistent access. Exploit token-creation privileges associated with service accounts to generate temporary credentials for high-privilege service accounts and exfiltrate infrastructure credentials, internal database passwords, and third-party API keys from cloud secret managers. Create unauthorized IAM and service accounts and inject SSH keys into compute instances for persistence. Create backdoor service accounts disguised as internal billing optimization utilities. Exploit vulnerabilities targeting LLM routing software, such as CVE-2026-40217 in LiteLLM, to escalate privileges. "The ultimate objective of LLMJacking is the monetization and resource-hijacking of foundation models, which actors achieve through token proxying, automated model streaming, and GPU hardware provisioning," Google said. "Threat actors also leveraged their access to host their own proxy endpoints and agentic workloads." UNC6993, for instance, has created additional API keys to scale their operations within victim cloud projects, racking up over $100,000 USD in billing charges. Some threat actors attempt to bypass rate limits by adopting a "burn and rotate" strategy that involves continuously creating and deleting short-lived service accounts The maturation of the LLMjacking ecosystem has also paved the way for the emergence of a new category of actors called LLM Mixers, highlighting a division of labor between attackers who establish initial access and those who manage downstream monetization infrastructure. LLM Mixers function as illicit routing gateways that proxy, aggregate, and resell unauthorized LLM access to other criminal actors via underground storefronts. One such service is Jet Night ("jet-night[.]com"), which offers an unlimited token plan with alleged access to a frontier model for approximately $60 per month. By fueling an illicit resale marketplace, it permits bad actors to siphon enterprise quotas while passing the billing costs to victims before compromises are detected. Jet Night is far from the only token routing offering. According to a report published by Broadcom-owned Symantec and Carbon Black last week, there exists a grey market relay service that installs the genuine OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code CLIs on enterprise systems, only to reconfigure them to route every request through third-party infrastructure instead of the vendors' own servers. The service is assessed to be active since at least early 2026, primarily impacting a dozen organizations located in Mainland China, along with multi-national subsidiaries based in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia. Targeted sectors include industrial automation, electronics manufacturing, semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, shipping, tire manufacturing, petrochemicals, and data center services. "Rather than building its own client software, the service repurposes the genuine CLI tools," Symantec said. "It installs them normally, then rewrites their configuration to switch sandboxing off, in Codex's case by setting it to 'danger-full-access,' and routes every request through its own servers instead of OpenAI's or Anthropic's." The service appears to mainly target markets where Anthropic and OpenAI do not operate, with the installation driven by an employee attempting to try out a Western AI coding assistant by turning to an unauthorized reseller. Notably, the service does not distribute a modified or trojanized client. Shortly after the legitimate install of the Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, users are likely instructed to run a one-line command to fetch fileless PowerShell or bash setup script from a lookalike domain ("vibe.aiok[.]me") that's used to override the configuration. The reconfiguration, which targets "~/.codex/config.toml" for Codex or "~/.claude/settings.json" for Claude Code, disables the CLI's execution sandbox, enables network access for the write sandbox, replaces the user's real API credentials with relay-issued tokens, and disables telemetry and error reporting. The script also checks the Windows locale setting to confirm it's running on a system in the region it serves before the setup is completed. It's suspected that the operators behind the service are not only circumventing regional restrictions imposed by Western AI vendors, but are also reselling capacity below market rates similar to Jet Night. Although there is no evidence to suggest that the service is abusing its position to harvest prompts entered by employees or fabricate or alter responses, the findings demonstrate the security risks associated with using such tools. "Threat actors will increasingly prioritize LLMJacking over traditional resource theft like cryptojacking, driven by the immediate, high-margin monetization enabled by emerging underground LLM Mixers," Google said. "As enterprises integrate higher-tier models and agentic workflows into production environments, cybercriminals will likely refine automated reconnaissance to target exposed API tokens and exploit vulnerabilities in model routing middleware."

1u80jo1.text: An attacker broke into the update system of the cPGuard security tool on November 2 and used it to send a malicious script to customers' Linux servers. The script installed a backdoor and collected password hashes and other sensitive files from servers that ran it, cPGuard maker OPSSHIELD said in an advisory. The attacker has since taken some of that data. cPGuard 5.88.25 and later versions remove the backdoor and the files the script left. Credentials the script copied may still work after the update, so any server that may have run the script also needs new passwords and keys. At 02:06 UTC, the attacker, who has not been identified, used compromised credentials to get into cPGuard's update system. The script went out in cPGuard versions 5.88.12 through 5.88.19. The attack was detected within 12 hours of those versions going out, according to OPSSHIELD. The company has cleared its infrastructure credentials and stopped the script from reaching more servers. It is still investigating how the attacker got the credentials. OPSSHIELD has not said how many servers installed one of these versions. Servers check for updates at intervals, so some may not have run the script. Admins can check whether a server installed an affected version by searching its update log: grep 'Successfully updated' /opt/cpguard/logs/install_log An entry for any version from 5.88.12 through 5.88.19 means the server installed an affected update. The entry alone does not show that the script ran or that data left the server. The server should still be treated as potentially compromised, even if it now runs 5.88.25 or later. A server with no matching entries, or with a missing or incomplete log, may still have run the script. Admins who are unsure can contact OPSSHIELD Support. The script collected these kinds of data, OPSSHIELD found: /etc/shadow and /etc/passwd, root's MariaDB or MySQL configuration (my.cnf), root's shell history, and the SSH authorization and known-hosts files for root. It may not have collected every file from every server, and the company is still working out what left each one. The /etc/shadow file stores one-way password hashes. Weak, common or previously leaked passwords can be recovered from those hashes by testing guesses offline, and even strong ones still need resetting. Secrets that may sit in the database configuration or shell history have no such hashing to protect them. The script uploaded what it collected to a licensing server run by OPSSHIELD itself, using a compromised account, so the attacker could pick it up later. OPSSHIELD has since secured that account. The attacker took 32 files from that server, each tied to one customer server, OPSSHIELD estimated late on November 2 UTC. The count covers only files known to have been taken, and it may change. It does not show how many servers may be involved in total. Beyond the data collection and the backdoor, OPSSHIELD has found no other malicious activity so far, a finding it says is not final. What cPGuard Admins Should Do Now OPSSHIELD asks admins to update every cPGuard server now and confirm the version: Run cpgcli update --start on each server. Run cpgcli --version and check that it reports 5.88.25 or later. If the update fails or the version is lower, contact OPSSHIELD Support. Admins should also take these steps for any server where the script ran or may have run: From a trusted recovery environment, reset the passwords for root and every other local Linux account that uses a password. From a trusted device, change any of those passwords that are also used on other systems. Rotate the server's database passwords, S3 access keys, DigitalOcean tokens and any secrets recorded in root's shell history. Replace the SSH private keys stored under /root/.ssh, and remove the matching old public keys from every system that trusts them. OPSSHIELD is not recommending a full reset or operating system rebuild as a routine step, and says that view could change as the investigation continues. Admins who find other signs of compromise, or cannot confirm a server is clean, should ask OPSSHIELD Support for a case-by-case review, which may lead to a rebuild. Separately, OPSSHIELD is releasing another update, as a precaution, that removes its support-access keys from cPGuard servers where they were added earlier. Support access is a cPGuard feature customers use to let OPSSHIELD staff into a server for troubleshooting. Granting it adds an SSH public key belonging to OPSSHIELD to the authorized_keys file for root, according to the company's documentation. OPSSHIELD has not said whether the private key that matches its support-access key was exposed in the attack. Files the Script Left Behind OPSSHIELD published these file names. The update removes the backdoor shell and the collection directory, so their absence after updating proves nothing about whether the script ran. File: cpguard-v58812-i91511.sh (the malicious script) File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511_sh (backdoor shell) Directory: /var/tmp/.cpg91511 (where the script gathered files) File: /var/tmp/.cpg91511/loot.tgz (archive the script prepared)

1px8vm.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 03, 2026Vulnerability / Linux Fixed kernels for a use-after-free vulnerability in the Linux kernel's IPv4 TCP code are now available for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8, 9, and 10, while Ubuntu's fixes for its three newest long-term-support releases remain in its opt-in testing channel with no date for a regular update. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-98432, can be reached by a remote, unauthenticated attacker and can lead to remote code execution, Red Hat and Canonical said. The Linux kernel's own CVE team rates the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. Red Hat, which initially rated it Moderate at 5.9, has raised its score to 9.8 and now calls it Critical. The bug has been present since Linux 4.4, and the upstream fix landed in October. What the Flaw Is When a server accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, the kernel passes IP options from the incoming request to the new socket without copying them. If the client retransmits its connection request while another processor still reads those options, the kernel can read memory it has already freed. An attacker triggers the race by sending connection requests that carry IPv4 Record Route or Timestamp options to any listening TCP port. No login is needed. IPv6 is not affected on the main path. Red Hat shipped RHSA-2026:93414 (RHEL 8), RHSA-2026:93412 (RHEL 9), and RHSA-2026:93413 (RHEL 10) on November 1. A reboot is needed after installing the update. RHEL Version Fixed Kernel Errata 8.10 4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10 RHSA-2026:93414 9.8 5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8 RHSA-2026:93412 10.2 6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2 RHSA-2026:93413 Canonical said on November 2 that fixes for Ubuntu 22.04 LTS, 24.04 LTS, and 26.04 LTS are in its -proposed pocket, an opt-in testing channel. Packages there do not install automatically. Canonical tests kernel updates across more than 2,000 certified servers and devices before releasing them to the regular update channel, and no release date has been given. Ubuntu Release -proposed Kernel Status 22.04 LTS (Jammy) 5.15.0-203.213 In -proposed 24.04 LTS (Noble) 6.8.0-149.149 In -proposed 26.04 LTS (Resolute) 7.0.0-43.43 In -proposed 20.04 / 18.04 / 16.04 Pending Administrators who need the fix before it reaches the regular channel can enable -proposed and install the kernel update by running: sudo add-apt-repository --component main --pocket proposed https://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu dpkg-query -W -f '${source:Package}\t${binary:Package}\n' | awk '$1 ~ "^linux-meta" { print $2 }' | xargs sudo apt install -t $(. /etc/os-release && echo $VERSION_CODENAME)-proposed --only-upgrade sudo reboot To check whether a system is running a fixed kernel, compare the output of uname -r against the versions in the tables above. Ubuntu 20.04, 18.04, and 16.04 have no fix yet. Older releases require Expanded Security Maintenance through Ubuntu Pro. Cloud, FIPS, and real-time kernel variants for Ubuntu are listed as work in progress on the Ubuntu CVE page with target versions, but Canonical's blog post covers only the generic kernel. Interim Mitigation Red Hat published an nftables rule on October 30 that drops inbound IPv4 TCP packets carrying IP options. The rule blocks the known trigger for the race but cannot fully prevent exploitation and may break workloads that depend on IPv4 options, Red Hat said. table inet cve_2026_98432 { chain input { type filter hook input priority -310; policy accept; ip protocol tcp ip hdrlength > 5 counter drop } } The filter applies only to the host where it is loaded. Traffic between containers on the same host can bypass it, a member of the CIQ kernel team noted on the oss-security mailing list. Several sources have recommended disabling Multipath TCP (MPTCP) as a workaround. The flaw is in the IPv4 TCP path, not in MPTCP, and that advice alone is not enough, Canonical said. "The Ubuntu Security Team believes that security updates are the only appropriate mitigation." Exploitation Status No vendor, CERT, or the kernel CVE team has reported attacks using this flaw. It was not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of the catalog's October 30 release. Anthropic said on October 27 that an unreleased, internal Claude research model wrote a remote root exploit for the flaw that works against Linux servers with an MPTCP listener, with no credentials and no user interaction. In its proof of concept, leaking a kernel address took 48 minutes and reaching a root shell took another 5 minutes. Anthropic has not published the exploit code. Proof-only code that triggers the race and detects the kernel echoing freed memory in a SYN-ACK has appeared on GitHub. It does not implement code execution. Amazon Linux scored the flaw 8.1 and rated it Important, saying the main outcome is a crash with possible memory corruption. Debian, Oracle Linux, and SUSE shipped fixes in October. Amazon Linux was fixed across all packages between October 24 and 30.

wlj457.text: Your team is remediating more vulnerabilities than ever, yet your breach risk has barely changed. You’re spending too much time and effort on exposures attackers may never exploit, while higher-risk exposures sit, waiting in the queue. Gartner®’s report on exposure prioritization states that fewer than 10% of vulnerabilities are exploited, yet most are treated as urgent. The report also argues that CVSS scores alone do not predict actual exploitation or business impact. Gartner predicts that by 2028, organizations that prioritize exposures using threat intelligence, asset context, exploitability modeling, and security control validation will reduce breach likelihood by at least 70% compared to their peers relying primarily on CVSS-based vulnerability prioritization. Let’s break down how each element works, and how the Picus Platform puts all four into practice. Severity-based prioritization made sense. Then it didn't. Severity-driven prioritization was an entirely rational response for the era it was built in: a static attack surface, scarce adversary tooling, and remediation capacity that exceeded disclosure volume. Suddenly, that world is gone. Enterprises face tens of thousands of new vulnerabilities a year across cloud, SaaS, identity, and supply chain modalities, and AI has compressed time-to-exploit from weeks or months to hours. Gartner is candid about why teams still anchor on severity, and it’s not a lack of awareness. In fact: legacy metrics compliance pressure, and fragmented ownership all reward what’s auditable over what’s legitimately impactful. The result is widespread prioritization paralysis, with significant resources being funneled into remediation activity, but with remarkably little measurable risk reduction to show for it. The smarter path is performing risk-based vulnerability management in its truest sense: measuring success by the exploitable exposures you’ve reduced, not the hypothetical vulnerabilities you’ve closed. The four elements, and the question each one answers Gartner’s framework rests on four pillars, and their value emerges only when added together. Sure, operationalizing one or two will bring you incremental gains, but integrating all four delivers significant reductions in both exposure windows and remediation fatigue. Each element answers a distinct question about an exposure: An exposure deserves urgent remediation only when all four answers converge. The model aligns directly with the prioritization and validation stages of continuous threat exposure management (CTEM): remediation is mobilized only after priorities are validated in context. Element 1: Threat Intelligence Threat intelligence brings the adversary’s perspective into prioritization by showing which exposures attackers are actually exploiting. In real-world environments, many high-severity vulnerabilities are never exploited. Attackers frequently weaponize moderately rated vulnerabilities because they are easier to exploit, affect widely used systems, or can be exploited reliably. Past exploitation evidence helps teams focus their remediation efforts on a smaller, higher-risk subset of the backlog. The operational challenge here is speed. Your team needs to use that intelligence to decide what to test and fix before a campaign reaches your environment. Track the time it takes to go from threat publication to testing and remediation. Element 2: Asset Context and Business Criticality An exploitable vulnerability becomes materially risky when it affects an asset that supports critical business functions, processes regulated data, or provides an easy pivot to higher-value systems. Without asset context, prioritization treats all assets as equal, and attention can easily drift to low-impact systems while crown-jewel exposures wait in the same queue. This context already lives in tools most teams own: scanners, CMDBs, cloud security platforms, and identity systems. The practical work is to both unify it and keep it current, so its impact reflects the asset as it’s defended today, not as it appears in an inventory. Element 3: Exploitability Modeling Exploit prediction models such as EPSS estimate how likely a vulnerability is to be exploited, based on patterns like exploit complexity, component prevalence, and disclosure-to-exploitation timelines. These models complement threat intelligence by surfacing latent and lingering risks: helping identify the exposures that are statistically likely to be exploited before exploitation is widely observed, enabling you to shift teams from a reactive to an anticipatory or even proactive stance. Statistical likelihood describes the world in general, not your organization’s unique environment. EPSS points to what’s probably exploitable somewhere; only validation proves what is exploitable here and now. Exploitability modeling works best as a filter that feeds validation, not as a final verdict. Gartner’s full report goes deeper into how EPSS, KEV and similar models should be weighted against threat intelligence and control validation. Download the Gartner report on exposure prioritization to read the complete analysis. Element 4: Security Control Validation This is the element most programs are missing. Security control validation evaluates each exposure against the defenses already deployed around it: segmentation, endpoint protection, detection coverage, and identity controls. An exposure that looks critical may be practically unreachable behind your existing defenses, while a less critical one on a poorly monitored asset may carry far more risk than its score suggests. Ignoring control context, Gartner warns, leads to systematic overestimation of risk and the wasted remediation efforts that follow it. Testing shows whether attackers can realistically exploit an exposure in your specific environment today. Gartner notes this capability can be achieved with adversarial exposure validation techniques: proving exploitability with evidence, through live attack execution where testing is safe, and attack-chain analysis against deployed controls where assets can’t be touched. How Picus Operationalizes All Four Elements into a Single Loop The sum here is indeed greater than its parts, but the four elements only deliver their full value when evaluated together. This is, not surprisingly, where most organizations struggle as vulnerability management grows into exposure management. Why? Because in most organizations, threat intelligence sits with one team, asset context with another, exploitability scores are in a scanner, and control effectiveness only shows up in periodic assessments. Four inputs in four places do not lead to one decision. Picus is named among the vendors in the 2026 Gartner® Market Guide for Adversarial Exposure Validation. The Picus Platform brings all four elements together in a continuous loop: Discover, Validate, Prioritize, and Mobilize. Here’s how the platform maps to each element. Security control validation deserves a closer look, because evidence is what turns the other three elements from assumptions into decisions. Picus Breach and Attack Simulation is one of three validation methods on the platform. Picus Autonomous Penetration Testing runs real exploit paths against reachable production assets and proves which ones lead to your critical systems. Picus Exposure Validation breaks each CVE into the techniques an attacker must use and tests every step against your existing controls on that asset, with no exploit fired, so even assets you can never test live get an evidence-backed verdict. Together, these three validation methods give every exposure one explainable, organization-specific rating. What Good Looks Like: Measuring the Shift If prioritization is working, you should be able to see it in three places: your controls hold up better, you respond faster, and your team spends its time on the exposures that matter, rather than wasting it on the ones that don’t. Here’s what our customers are reporting. Within three months of deploying Picus, their security controls are blocking or detecting roughly twice as many attacks as before. Response time to emerging threats drops by 89%. Missed remediation deadlines on high and critical vulnerabilities fall by 92%, because the queue now holds only the exposures proven to be exploitable. One customer cut their critical ticket backlog by 98%. And the full cycle, from a new threat or change being detected to actual validated findings landing with the right team, runs under six hours. A CISO at our 2026 Validation Summit put it simply: While a severity score is a useful label for sorting, the smarter strategy is to shut down those attack paths that could actually hurt your business. The numbers above back this up. Exposure Prioritization Is a Risk Decision. Make It With Evidence. Gartner frames exposure prioritization as a risk decision, and we agree. Each of the four elements answers one part of it: threat intelligence tells you whether the exposure matters to an attacker, asset context tells you what it would cost you, exploitability modeling tells you how likely it is to take place, and security control validation tells you whether it could actually happen here.
